title: Upscaling LiDAR: From Airborne to Spaceborne
text: How do we bridge the gap between the centimeter-scale precision of airborne and drone LiDAR and the global but sparse footprints of spaceborne GEDI?

title: Upscaling LiDAR: From Airborne to Spaceborne
text:
1 · The Scaling Problem
LiDAR-based forest monitoring operates across a fundamental scale hierarchy that spans five orders of magnitude in spatial extent — from individual tree crowns measured by terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) at sub-centimeter resolution, to wall-to-wall continental coverage of 3DEP airborne LiDAR at ~1–10 pts/m², to the 25 m circular footprints of GEDI spaced ~600 m apart across the global tropics and temperate zone. Each tier of this hierarchy captures different aspects of forest structure, and no single platform can simultaneously deliver the spatial density, coverage extent, and temporal frequency required for global carbon accounting.
The core challenge of LiDAR upscaling is to propagate structural information measured precisely at small scales — tree height, crown volume, canopy density, gap fraction — to the regional and global scales where forest carbon policy operates, while preserving the accuracy inherited from the high-fidelity source data.

The spatial mismatch is severe: a single 3DEP ALS tile at 1 pt/m² over a 1 km² area contains ~1,000,000 returns; GEDI provides roughly 3–5 footprints across the same area, each a 25 m circle. The information density ratio is approximately 10,000:1. Upscaling is therefore fundamentally a statistical inference problem — how to learn from the dense but spatially limited ALS record and extrapolate to the globally sparse but spatially extensive GEDI sampling.

title: Upscaling LiDAR: From Airborne to Spaceborne
text:
3 · GEDI Waveform Simulation from ALS
Before upscaling can proceed, the two sensor types must be placed on a common footing. The GEDI Simulator (Hancock et al., 2019) allows full-waveform GEDI returns to be synthesized from existing ALS point clouds by convolving the 3D point distribution within a simulated 25 m footprint with the instrument’s Gaussian pulse, noise model, and detection threshold. This produces simulated GEDI waveforms and derived RH metrics (RH25, RH50, RH75, RH95, RH98, RH100) from ALS data, enabling direct metric-to-metric comparison at the same location.
Key applications of GEDI simulation from 3DEP / NEON ALS:

Calibration: Simulated GEDI metrics from ALS are compared to real GEDI acquisitions at co-located footprints to assess bias introduced by GEDI’s noise model, sensitivity threshold, and tandem-beam geometry. Studies consistently find that GEDI RH98 overestimates maximum canopy height by 1–3 m in closed-canopy boreal forests due to noise-induced apparent ground returns above the true canopy (Hofton et al., 2020).
Allometric calibration transfer: ALS-based AGB allometries (calibrated against field plots) can be transferred to GEDI metrics by expressing the allometry in terms of simulated RH metrics, rather than refitting with sparse GEDI footprint–plot pairs.
Filling GEDI gaps: Cloud cover and topographic shadowing create systematic gaps in GEDI coverage. ALS simulation allows gap-filling in areas with existing airborne coverage.

Foundational papers: - Blair & Hofton (1999) — original large-footprint waveform simulation framework - Hancock et al. (2019) — GEDI Simulator release; benchmark against 3DEP over Pacific Northwest - Hofton et al. (2020) — GEDI calibration using airborne waveform LiDAR

title: Upscaling LiDAR: From Airborne to Spaceborne
text:
4 · Methodological Frameworks for Upscaling

4.1 Area-Based Approach Extended to GEDI
The Area-Based Approach (ABA) is the standard methodology for ALS-based forest inventory: field plots provide ground-truth AGB or basal area, ALS-derived metrics (height percentiles, canopy cover, density indices) extracted over plot footprints serve as predictors, and a regression or machine learning model is trained and applied wall-to-wall. The ABA was developed for small-area operational forest inventory and typically achieves RMSE of 15–35 Mg ha⁻¹ for AGB depending on forest type.
Extending ABA to GEDI involves two stages: 1. ALS → field calibration: Train an ALS-based AGB model using plot data 2. ALS → GEDI transfer: Express ALS-derived AGB predictions as a function of GEDI RH metrics within simulated footprints, yielding a GEDI-native allometric model
This two-step transfer is used in the GEDI L4A algorithm (Duncanson et al., 2022), which employs 10 continent- and biome-specific models relating GEDI RH metrics to AGB, each calibrated using ALS-derived AGB estimates from co-located field-validated airborne surveys. The 3DEP program has contributed substantially to L4A calibration datasets across the contiguous United States.



4.2 GEDI as Training Labels for Wall-to-Wall Fusion
The most widely adopted upscaling pathway for global applications uses GEDI footprint-level estimates as sparse but globally representative training labels, fused with wall-to-wall optical or SAR imagery to predict at unseen locations. This approach shifts the core problem from LiDAR data fusion to machine learning generalization.
Canonical workflows:
Canopy height (Lang et al., 2022 — ETH/Meta): GEDI L2A RH98 canopy height → training labels; Sentinel-2 spectral-temporal metrics → features; a global CNN (SegFormer-based) trained on ~1 billion pixels predicts 10 m canopy height wall-to-wall. Validated against NEON ALS and 3DEP tiles; global RMSE ~2.8 m.
Canopy height (Potapov et al., 2021 — NASA/UMD): GEDI L2A canopy height + Landsat 8 OLI annual composites → gradient boosting regression tree → 30 m global canopy height. Explicitly uses 3DEP-derived ALS metrics as independent validation across the CONUS.
Forest AGB (Wang et al., 2022): GEDI L4A footprint AGB → training; Landsat + Sentinel-1 SAR + Sentinel-2 + SRTM topography → features; deep learning (CNN + XGBoost ensemble) → 30 m global AGB. Achieves rRMSE ~30–45% globally; higher error in tropical dense-canopy forests.
Key design choices that affect upscaling accuracy: - Temporal matching: ALS and GEDI data must be from the same or nearby years to avoid change-induced mismatch; 3DEP tiles from 2012–2019 may predate GEDI (2019–present) by up to 7 years in fast-changing forests - Feature space coverage: The optical/SAR feature space of training GEDI footprints must cover the full range of the prediction domain; tropical forests with high AGB but few GEDI samples are systematically underrepresented - Saturation: Both GEDI RH metrics and SAR backscatter saturate above ~150–200 Mg ha⁻¹ AGB — a fundamental ceiling on prediction accuracy in high-biomass forests



4.3 Hierarchical / Multi-Scale Fusion
A more rigorous framework treats the upscaling as a hierarchical geostatistical problem, explicitly modeling the spatial covariance structure at each scale. The GEDI L4B gridded product uses a Hybrid Model-Based Geostatistical (HMB) estimator (Saarela et al., 2018) that:

Predicts AGB at each GEDI L4A footprint using the biome-specific allometric model
Fits a geostatistical model (variogram) to the spatial correlation of L4A residuals
Uses kriging to interpolate predictions to a 1 km grid with explicit uncertainty propagation

This framework rigorously propagates uncertainty from the allometric model through the spatial interpolation, producing per-pixel standard errors alongside the mean AGBD estimate. 3DEP-derived ALS data from the CONUS contribute to the empirical variogram estimation and out-of-sample validation.



4.4 Transfer Learning and Domain Adaptation
A critical challenge in upscaling is geographic extrapolation: a model trained on GEDI footprints in temperate US forests (well-covered by 3DEP) must predict accurately in tropical forests, boreal zones, or arid woodlands with different structure–spectral relationships. Standard random forest and XGBoost models degrade substantially when applied outside their training domain.
Emerging approaches:

Domain-adversarial training: Forces the feature extractor to learn representations invariant to geographic domain (source = 3DEP/NEON-rich regions; target = tropical regions with only GEDI and optical data), improving cross-domain AGB transfer (Dalponte et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022)
Self-supervised pre-training on optical imagery: Pre-train a large vision model on global Sentinel-2/Landsat imagery without labels (SatMAE, SeCo), then fine-tune with GEDI labels — improves generalization to unseen biomes
Physics-informed constraints: Add loss penalties that enforce known relationships (AGB increases monotonically with canopy height within PFT) to prevent physically implausible predictions in novel environments

text:
5 · USGS 3DEP as the Upscaling Bridge
The USGS 3D Elevation Program (3DEP) occupies a uniquely important position in the ALS-to-GEDI upscaling chain for North American applications. As of FY2025, 3DEP has achieved ~90% CONUS coverage at Quality Level 2 (QL2, ≥2 pts/m²) or better, making it the largest contiguous ALS dataset available anywhere.
Specific contributions of 3DEP to GEDI upscaling:







Role
Mechanism




GEDI L4A calibration
3DEP-derived AGB estimates used as calibration targets in temperate US biomes


GEDI waveform validation
Simulated GEDI waveforms from 3DEP compared to real GEDI acquisitions


Vertical accuracy assessment
3DEP DTM used to assess GEDI ground elevation errors in sloped terrain


Gap-filling
3DEP fills GEDI gaps in high-latitude CONUS (>51.6°N not covered by GEDI)


Temporal change detection
Multi-year 3DEP acquisitions detect post-disturbance height change independent of GEDI


Training data for ML models
3DEP tiles provide dense labeled AGB/height data for supervised learning



Spatial coverage progression: The animated 3DEP coverage map (FY2013–FY2025) shows steady annual expansion, with priority given to wildfire-prone western states (California, Oregon, Washington) and flood-prone river corridors. By FY2025, 3DEP provides the most comprehensive single-nation ALS archive ever assembled.
Resolution hierarchy within 3DEP: - QL0 — experimental, >8 pts/m² (urban, engineering) - QL1 — ≥8 pts/m², ≤12.5 cm vertical RMSE (precision mapping) - QL2 — ≥2 pts/m², ≤10 cm vertical RMSE (national standard) - QL3 — ≥0.5 pts/m², ≤20 cm vertical RMSE (legacy coverage)
For upscaling to GEDI, QL2 and above provide sufficient density to reliably simulate GEDI waveforms and estimate canopy height percentiles at 25 m footprint scale.

title: Upscaling LiDAR: From Airborne to Spaceborne
text:
6 · Key Challenges

6.1 Sensor Physics Mismatch
GEDI uses a full-waveform Gaussian beam with a 25 m diameter and ~6 ns pulse width, recording the continuous distribution of energy returns with height. ALS systems typically record discrete returns (first, last, or multiple) from a narrow beam (0.1–0.3 m footprint). Converting ALS discrete returns to simulate GEDI waveforms requires careful modeling of the beam divergence, multiple scattering, and noise floor — errors in this simulation propagate directly into calibration offsets.


6.2 Saturation in Dense Canopy
Both ALS-derived canopy height metrics and GEDI RH metrics show saturation at high AGB values (typically >150 Mg ha⁻¹ in tropical forests, >200 Mg ha⁻¹ in temperate conifers). This is because the LiDAR signal is dominated by the uppermost canopy layer, with little sensitivity to biomass accumulated in lower strata or large trunk volumes. Saturation introduces systematic underestimation of AGB in the most carbon-rich forests — precisely those of greatest interest for climate policy.
Mitigations: L-band SAR backscatter (ALOS PALSAR) remains sensitive at higher AGB; combining GEDI RH metrics with SAR reduces saturation bias. The forthcoming ESA BIOMASS P-band SAR mission is specifically designed to overcome saturation up to ~500 Mg ha⁻¹.


6.3 Temporal Mismatch
3DEP ALS acquisitions occurred over 2012–2025; GEDI operates 2019–present. In areas with active forest management, fire disturbance, or insect-induced mortality, structural changes between the ALS acquisition and the GEDI overpass can introduce calibration errors. Temporal correction using Landsat/Sentinel-based disturbance maps (LandTrendr, LCMS) is an active area of development.


6.4 Slope and Terrain Effects
GEDI footprint returns on steep slopes appear shifted in height because the circular footprint intercepts ground at multiple elevations. This introduces apparent height errors that can exceed 5 m on slopes >25°, substantially degrading canopy height retrieval in mountainous terrain. Slope correction algorithms exist (Tang & Armston, 2019) but require accurate DTMs — which 3DEP can provide.


6.5 Cloud Cover Gaps
GEDI accumulates coverage over multiple orbital passes, but persistent cloud cover in tropical regions (Amazon, Congo, Southeast Asia) creates systematic acquisition gaps in the very forests that matter most for global carbon accounting. ALS-based upscaling provides an independent path to wall-to-wall mapping in cloud-affected regions.

title: Upscaling LiDAR: From Airborne to Spaceborne
text:
7 · Emerging Directions
Multi-mission fusion: Combining GEDI (25 m waveform, ±51.6°) with ICESat-2 ATL08 (global, ±88°, photon-counting) extends LiDAR-based canopy height estimation to boreal and Arctic forests beyond GEDI’s orbital limit. ICESat-2 and GEDI overlapped in 2019–2023, enabling cross-calibration studies.
GEDI continuity and GEDI-II: The original GEDI mission is planned for decommissioning; GEDI-II (under development) would extend the orbital inclination and improve coverage. Meanwhile, commercial spaceborne LiDAR platforms (e.g., Planet’s forest carbon products) are beginning to fill gaps.
Foundation models for forest structure: Large pre-trained vision transformers trained on multi-source remote sensing data (imagery + LiDAR + SAR) are emerging as universal upscaling engines — a single model can be fine-tuned for canopy height, AGB, or species composition with minimal additional labeled data.
Drone LiDAR as calibration nodes: UAS-LiDAR systems (DJI Zenmuse L1/L2, Riegl miniVUX) are increasingly used to acquire plot-level 3D point clouds at <5 cm resolution, bridging the gap between TLS (sub-centimeter, single tree) and ALS (plot to regional). Drone acquisitions co-located with GEDI footprints provide the highest-quality calibration data possible — capturing complete 3D crown structure within the exact 25 m footprint geometry.

title: Upscaling LiDAR: From Airborne to Spaceborne
text:
8 · Summary
The upscaling chain from drone/ALS LiDAR to GEDI represents one of the most active frontiers in forest carbon monitoring. The canonical pathway — field plots → ALS calibration → GEDI allometry → optical/SAR fusion → wall-to-wall map — has produced the first generation of globally consistent, meter-scale canopy height and biomass products. 3DEP’s continental ALS coverage is the backbone of this chain in North America, providing both the calibration data for GEDI allometries and the independent validation benchmark for global products.
Outstanding challenges — sensor physics mismatch, saturation, temporal inconsistency, and geographic extrapolation — are being addressed through waveform simulation, multi-source fusion, and domain-adaptive machine learning. The next decade, with NISAR (L+S band SAR), BIOMASS (P-band SAR), and potential GEDI continuity missions, promises to resolve the saturation problem and extend LiDAR-based biomass monitoring to the full global forest carbon stock.

Forests and urban ecosystems are simultaneously shaped by climate variability, disturbance regimes, and human land management. Understanding how these forces interact — and quantifying their effects on carbon stocks, biodiversity, and human well-being — requires observations spanning from individual tree crowns to global scales, and methods ranging from empirical field measurements to process-based simulation.

Multi-platform remote sensing (airborne LiDAR, spaceborne LiDAR, optical, radar) to characterize ecosystem structure across spatial scales
Field inventory data (FIA, NEON) to calibrate and validate remote sensing-derived estimates
Statistical and machine learning models to map ecosystem properties and detect change at landscape to continental scales

title: LiDAR Metric Calculation: Canopy Structure, Complexity, and Urban Buildings
text: Following the pre-processing pipeline, this post covers extraction of structural metrics from the cleaned, height-normalised point cloud — shown in parallel across lidR, lasR, and Python (laspy + numpy / scipy / shapely).

title: LiDAR Metric Calculation: Canopy Structure, Complexity, and Urban Buildings
text:
Part 1 — Canopy Height Metrics
Height percentiles characterise the vertical distribution of the canopy and are the backbone of LiDAR-based AGB and canopy height modelling.

1.1 Height Percentiles and Basic Statistics

lidRlasRPython


height_metrics <- function(z) {
  p  <- c(10, 25, 50, 75, 90, 95, 99)
  hp <- as.list(quantile(z, p / 100))
  names(hp) <- paste0("H", p)
  c(
    hp,
    Hmean = mean(z),
    Hmax  = max(z),
    Hsd   = sd(z),
    Hcv   = sd(z) / mean(z),
    Hskew = moments::skewness(z),
    Hkurt = moments::kurtosis(z),
    Hqm   = sqrt(mean(z^2))
  )
}

# Rasterised at 20 × 20 m grid (exclude returns ≤ 2 m)
metrics_grid <- pixel_metrics(las, ~height_metrics(Height[Height > 2]), res = 20)

# Point-cloud level (single plot or tile)
metrics_plot <- cloud_metrics(las, ~height_metrics(Height[Height > 2]))


# height_metrics() is defined identically to the lidR version above.
# Pass it inside rasterize() — lasR streams the tile and evaluates
# the formula per grid cell without loading the full tile.

pipeline <-
  reader_las() +
  rasterize(
    res     = 20,
    metrics = ~height_metrics(Height[Height > 2]),
    ofile   = "height_metrics_20m.tif"
  )

exec(pipeline, on = "path/to/folder/", ncores = 4L, chunk = 500, buffer = 10)


def height_metrics(h):
    """Height above ground array → dict of metrics. h should be pre-filtered (h > 2)."""
    if len(h) < 5:
        return None
    percs = np.percentile(h, [10, 25, 50, 75, 90, 95, 99])
    return {
        "H10":   percs[0], "H25": percs[1], "H50": percs[2],
        "H75":   percs[3], "H90": percs[4], "H95": percs[5], "H99": percs[6],
        "Hmean": h.mean(),
        "Hmax":  h.max(),
        "Hsd":   h.std(),
        "Hcv":   h.std() / h.mean() if h.mean() > 0 else np.nan,
        "Hskew": stats.skew(h),
        "Hkurt": stats.kurtosis(h),
        "Hqm":   np.sqrt(np.mean(h**2))
    }

# ── Pixel-level (20 m grid) ────────────────────────────────────────
def pixel_metrics(x, y, H, func, res=20):
    """Apply func over a regular res × res grid; returns dict of 2D arrays."""
    h_filt = H > 2
    xmin, xmax = x.min(), x.max()
    ymin, ymax = y.min(), y.max()
    cols = max(1, int(np.ceil((xmax - xmin) / res)))
    rows = max(1, int(np.ceil((ymax - ymin) / res)))
    ci = np.clip(((x - xmin) / res).astype(int), 0, cols - 1)
    ri = np.clip(((ymax - y) / res).astype(int), 0, rows - 1)
    out = {}
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            mask = (ri == r) & (ci == c) & h_filt
            if mask.sum() < 5:
                continue
            m = func(H[mask])
            if m is None:
                continue
            for k, v in m.items():
                if k not in out:
                    out[k] = np.full((rows, cols), np.nan)
                out[k][r, c] = v
    return out

grid = pixel_metrics(x, y, H, height_metrics, res=20)











Metric
Formula
Ecological meaning




H50
50th percentile
Median canopy height — robust central tendency


H95 / H99
95th / 99th percentile
Dominant / emergent height; proxy for top-of-canopy


Hmean
\(\bar{H}\)
Mean canopy height — strongly correlated with AGB


Hsd
\(\sigma_H\)
Vertical spread — indicator of structural heterogeneity


Hcv
\(\sigma_H / \bar{H}\)
Scale-free variability — useful across biomes


Hskew
\(\mu_3 / \sigma^3\)
Positive skew = bottom-heavy profile (young/regrowth)


Hqm
\(\sqrt{\bar{H^2}}\)
Quadratic mean — more sensitive to tall trees than Hmean









Tip



H99 vs Hmax: Hmax is the single tallest point and is highly susceptible to surviving noise. H99 is far more robust and is what most published AGB models use.





1.2 Canopy Cover and Gap Fraction

lidRlasRPython


cover_metrics <- function(z, rn, threshold = 2) {
  list(
    CC       = mean(z >= threshold),
    GF       = mean(z < threshold),
    CC_first = mean(z[rn == 1] >= threshold)
  )
}

cover_grid <- pixel_metrics(
  las,
  ~cover_metrics(Height, ReturnNumber, threshold = 2),
  res = 20
)


pipeline <-
  reader_las() +
  rasterize(
    res     = 20,
    metrics = ~list(
      CC       = mean(Height >= 2),
      GF       = mean(Height <  2),
      CC_first = mean(Height[ReturnNumber == 1] >= 2)
    ),
    ofile   = "cover_20m.tif"
  )

exec(pipeline, on = "path/to/folder/", ncores = 4L, chunk = 500, buffer = 10)


def cover_metrics(h, ret, threshold=2.0):
    n_total  = len(h)
    n_above  = np.sum(h >= threshold)
    first    = ret == 1
    return {
        "CC":       n_above / n_total if n_total > 0 else np.nan,
        "GF":       1 - n_above / n_total if n_total > 0 else np.nan,
        "CC_first": np.mean(h[first] >= threshold) if first.sum() > 0 else np.nan
    }

# Grid version — uses the same pixel_metrics() helper from above
def cover_func(h):
    return cover_metrics(h, ret[H > -999], threshold=2.0)



Canopy cover (CC) from LiDAR:
\[CC = \frac{n_{\text{returns} \geq h_t}}{n_{\text{total returns}}} \times 100\%\]
Gap fraction (GF = 1 − CC) as a proxy for LAI via Beer-Lambert:
\[\text{LAI} \approx -\frac{\ln(\text{GF})}{k}, \quad k \approx 0.5\]

Part 2 — Vertical Density and Profile Metrics

2.1 Density by Height Stratum

lidRlasRPython


density_profile <- function(z) {
  breaks <- c(0, 0.5, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, Inf)
  labels <- c("G", "S0.5", "S2", "S5", "S10", "S20", "S30")
  strata <- cut(z[z >= 0], breaks = breaks, labels = labels, right = FALSE)
  tab    <- table(strata)
  prop   <- as.list(prop.table(tab))
  names(prop) <- paste0("D_", names(prop))
  prop
}

density_grid <- pixel_metrics(las, ~density_profile(Height), res = 20)


# density_profile() defined as above; referenced inside rasterize()
pipeline <-
  reader_las() +
  rasterize(
    res     = 20,
    metrics = ~density_profile(Height),
    ofile   = "density_profile_20m.tif"
  )

exec(pipeline, on = "path/to/folder/", ncores = 4L, chunk = 500, buffer = 10)


def density_profile(h):
    h   = h[h >= 0]
    if len(h) == 0:
        return None
    breaks = [0, 0.5, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, np.inf]
    labels = ["G", "S0.5", "S2", "S5", "S10", "S20", "S30"]
    counts = np.histogram(h, bins=breaks)[0]
    total  = counts.sum()
    return {f"D_{lbl}": c / total for lbl, c in zip(labels, counts)}






Ratio
Meaning




D_S10 + D_S20 + D_S30
Upper canopy dominance


D_G + D_S0.5
Ground / near-ground proportion (bare soil indicator)


D_S2 / D_S10
Understory-to-upper-canopy ratio





2.2 Canopy Layer Separation

lidRlasRPython


layer_metrics <- function(z) {
  list(
    P_above2  = mean(z >= 2),
    P_above10 = mean(z >= 10),
    P_above20 = mean(z >= 20),
    ratio_sub = mean(z >= 2 & z < 10) / max(mean(z >= 10), 1e-6)
  )
}

layer_grid <- pixel_metrics(las, ~layer_metrics(Height), res = 20)


pipeline <-
  reader_las() +
  rasterize(
    res     = 20,
    metrics = ~list(
      P_above2  = mean(Height >= 2),
      P_above10 = mean(Height >= 10),
      P_above20 = mean(Height >= 20),
      ratio_sub = mean(Height >= 2 & Height < 10) /
                  max(mean(Height >= 10), 1e-6)
    ),
    ofile = "layers_20m.tif"

title: LiDAR Metric Calculation: Canopy Structure, Complexity, and Urban Buildings
text:
Part 3 — Structural Complexity Metrics

3.1 Rumple Index (RI)
\[RI = \frac{A_{3D}}{A_{2D}}\]
\(A_{3D}\) — triangulated canopy surface area (TIN from first returns); \(A_{2D}\) — projected footprint. A flat uniform canopy has \(RI \approx 1\); a complex multi-layered canopy has \(RI \gg 1\).

lidRlasRPython


# lidR computes RI from a Canopy Height Model raster
chm <- rasterize_canopy(las, res = 1, algorithm = p2r(subcircle = 0.2))
ri  <- rumple_index(chm)

  las,
  ~list(RI = rumple_index(
    rasterize_canopy(las, res = 1, algorithm = p2r()))),
  res = 50
)


# lasR has a dedicated chm() stage; RI is computed on the output raster
# using lidR::rumple_index() after exec() (not inside the pipeline).

  reader_las() +
  chm(res = 1, ofile = "chm_1m.tif")

# Post-process: load the CHM raster and compute RI per block
chm_r <- terra::rast("chm_1m.tif")
ri    <- lidR::rumple_index(chm_r)


def rumple_index_py(x, y, z, res=1.0):
    """Compute RI via Delaunay triangulation of first-return canopy surface."""
    # Keep only first returns (or highest-z per cell as a proxy)
    xi  = np.floor(x / res).astype(int)
    yi  = np.floor(y / res).astype(int)
    key = xi * 1_000_000_007 + yi
    _, top = np.unique(key, return_index=True)   # one pt per cell = highest
    px, py, pz = x[top], y[top], z[top]

    if len(px) < 4:
        return np.nan

    pts2d = np.column_stack([px, py])
    tri   = Delaunay(pts2d)

    # 3D surface area via cross product for each triangle
    verts = np.column_stack([px, py, pz])
    a3d   = 0.0
    for s in tri.simplices:
        v  = verts[s]
        ab = v[1] - v[0]
        ac = v[2] - v[0]
        a3d += np.linalg.norm(np.cross(ab, ac)) / 2

    a2d = (px.max() - px.min()) * (py.max() - py.min())
    return a3d / a2d if a2d > 0 else np.nan

ri = rumple_index_py(x, y, H, res=1.0)

Important



RI is resolution-sensitive: a 0.25 m CHM captures branch-level rugosity; a 5 m CHM smooths it. Always report CHM resolution alongside RI.





3.2 Canopy Relief Ratio (CRR)
\[CRR = \frac{\bar{H} - H_{\min}}{H_{\max} - H_{\min}}\]

lidRlasRPython

def crr_metric(h):
    h = h[h >= 0]
    if len(h) < 3:
        return {"CRR": np.nan}
    return {"CRR": (h.mean() - h.min()) / (h.max() - h.min() + 1e-6)}



Low CRR (< 0.4) → bottom-heavy (open/low-stature); high CRR (> 0.6) → top-heavy (dense tall closed canopy).



3.3 Vertical Complexity Index (VCI) — Shannon Entropy
\[VCI = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i \ln(p_i)\]
Normalised VCI = VCI / ln(n) ranges 0–1 (0 = single layer; 1 = uniform vertical distribution).

lidRlasRPython


vci_metric <- function(z, n_strata = 10) {
  z     <- z[z >= 0 & z < 80]
  strat <- cut(z, breaks = seq(0, 80, length.out = n_strata + 1),
               include.lowest = TRUE)
  p     <- prop.table(table(strat))
  p     <- p[p > 0]
  vci   <- -sum(p * log(p))
  list(VCI = vci, VCI_norm = vci / log(n_strata))
}

def vci_metric(h, n_strata=10):
    h = h[(h >= 0) & (h < 80)]
    if len(h) < 5:
        return {"VCI": np.nan, "VCI_norm": np.nan}
    edges  = np.linspace(0, 80, n_strata + 1)
    counts = np.histogram(h, bins=edges)[0]
    p      = counts / counts.sum()
    p      = p[p > 0]
    vci    = -np.sum(p * np.log(p))
    return {"VCI": vci, "VCI_norm": vci / np.log(n_strata)}

def bimodality_coefficient(h):
    n = len(h)
    if n < 4:
        return np.nan
    sk = stats.skew(h)
    ku = stats.kurtosis(h)   # Fisher (excess) kurtosis
    return (sk**2 + 1) / (ku + 3 * (n - 1)**2 / max((n - 2) * (n - 3), 1))

def shape_metrics(h):
    h = h[h >= 0]
    if len(h) < 4:
        return None
    return {
        "Hskew":  stats.skew(h),
        "Hkurt":  stats.kurtosis(h),
        "Hbimod": bimodality_coefficient(h),
        "Hrange": h.max() - h.min()
    }

4.2 Roof Geometry and Complexity

roof_metrics <- function(x, y, z) {
  pts      <- cbind(x, y, z)
  eig      <- eigen(cov(pts))
  normal   <- eig$vectors[, 3]
  slope    <- acos(abs(normal[3])) * 180 / pi
  list(
    roof_slope_mean = slope,
    roof_roughness  = sd(z - mean(z))
  )
}

def roof_metrics(x, y, h):
    if len(h) < 6:
        return None
    pts    = np.column_stack([x, y, h])
    # PCA: eigenvector of smallest eigenvalue = surface normal
    _, evecs = np.linalg.eigh(np.cov(pts.T))
    normal   = evecs[:, 0]
    slope    = np.degrees(np.arccos(np.abs(normal[2])))
    return {
        "roof_slope_mean": slope,
        "roof_roughness":  np.std(h - h.mean())
    }

4.3 Building Footprint and Volume

lidRlasRPython


building_footprint_metrics <- function(x, y, z) {
  pts2d          <- st_sfc(st_multipoint(cbind(x, y)))
  hull           <- st_convex_hull(pts2d)
  footprint_area <- as.numeric(st_area(hull))
  perimeter      <- as.numeric(
    st_length(st_cast(hull, "MULTILINESTRING")))
  height_p95     <- quantile(z, 0.95)
  volume         <- footprint_area * height_p95
  compactness    <- 4 * pi * footprint_area / perimeter^2
  list(
    footprint_m2 = footprint_area,
    perimeter_m  = perimeter,
    compactness  = compactness,
    volume_m3    = volume,
    FAR          = volume / footprint_area
  )
}

# Footprint / volume require 2D convex hull per building — not
# directly supported inside rasterize(). Typical workflow:
#   1) Run exec() to get the CHM and a classified raster.
#   2) Vectorise building blobs with terra::patches() or sf operations.
#   3) For each polygon, extract building points and compute metrics in R.

def building_footprint_metrics(x, y, h):
    if len(h) < 4:
        return None
    pts2d = np.column_stack([x, y])
    try:
        hull = ConvexHull(pts2d)
    except Exception:
        return None
    # In scipy 2D ConvexHull: hull.volume = area, hull.area = perimeter
    footprint_area = hull.volume
    perimeter      = hull.area
    h_p95          = np.percentile(h, 95)
    volume         = footprint_area * h_p95
    compactness    = 4 * np.pi * footprint_area / perimeter**2
    return {
        "footprint_m2": footprint_area,
        "perimeter_m":  perimeter,
        "compactness":  compactness,
        "volume_m3":    volume,
        "FAR":          volume / footprint_area
    }

# Approximate SVF via horizon scanning (simplified)
def svf_approx(ndsm, radius_px=50, n_dirs=36):
    rows, cols = ndsm.shape
    svf_out    = np.full_like(ndsm, np.nan, dtype=float)
    angles     = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, n_dirs, endpoint=False)
    r_range    = np.arange(1, radius_px + 1)
    for i in range(rows):
        for j in range(cols):
            max_sin2 = 0.0
            for a in angles:
                ri = (i + r_range * np.sin(a)).astype(int)
                ci = (j + r_range * np.cos(a)).astype(int)
                valid = (ri >= 0) & (ri < rows) & (ci >= 0) & (ci < cols)
                if valid.any():
                    elev = ndsm[ri[valid], ci[valid]] / r_range[valid]
                    max_sin2 += np.sin(np.arctan(elev.max()))**2
            svf_out[i, j] = 1 - max_sin2 / n_dirs
    return svf_out

def compute_urban_metrics(las):
    x   = np.array(las.x)
    y   = np.array(las.y)
    H   = np.array(las.Height)
    cls = np.array(las.classification)

    veg_mask = np.isin(cls, [4, 5])
    bld_mask = cls == 6

    H_veg = H[veg_mask & (H >= 0)]
    H_bld = H[bld_mask]

    veg_m = {
        "H95":   np.percentile(H_veg, 95) if len(H_veg) > 0 else np.nan,
        "Hmean": H_veg.mean() if len(H_veg) > 0 else np.nan,
        "CC":    np.mean(H_veg >= 2) if len(H_veg) > 0 else np.nan,
        **vci_metric(H_veg),
        **crr_metric(H_veg)
    }
    bld_m = {
        **(building_height_metrics(H_bld) or {}),
        **(roof_metrics(x[bld_mask], y[bld_mask], H_bld) or {}),
        **(building_footprint_metrics(x[bld_mask], y[bld_mask], H_bld) or {})
    }
    return {"vegetation": veg_m, "buildings": bld_m}

GEDI L4A converts full-waveform LiDAR returns into footprint-level above-ground biomass density (AGBD) estimates using allometric models trained on forest inventory data. Each footprint covers ~25 m in diameter with ~600 m cross-track spacing.
This post validates GEDI L4A AGBD at NEON SCBI — Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute, Front Royal, Virginia — against two independent biomass estimates derived from airborne LiDAR acquired within the same temporal window.

title: GEDI L4A Above-Ground Biomass at NEON SCBI: Comparison with NEON AOP and 3DEP Allometric Estimates
text:
Step 3 — Extract AGBD from HDF5
GEDI L4A files follow the same 8-beam HDF5 structure as L2A, with AGBD and its 90% prediction interval stored per footprint.

extract_l4a <- function(h5_path, region) {
  h5    <- H5File$new(h5_path, mode="r")
  beams <- c("BEAM0000","BEAM0001","BEAM0010","BEAM0011",
             "BEAM0101","BEAM0110","BEAM1000","BEAM1011")

  results <- lapply(beams, function(beam) {
    if (!beam %in% names(h5)) return(NULL)
    tryCatch({
      b <- h5[[beam]]
      data.frame(
        lon        = b[["lon_lowestmode"]][],
        lat        = b[["lat_lowestmode"]][],
        agbd       = b[["agbd"]][],
        agbd_lower = b[["agbd_pi_lower"]][],
        agbd_upper = b[["agbd_pi_upper"]][],
        quality    = b[["l4_quality_flag"]][],
        degrade    = b[["degrade_flag"]][],
        beam       = beam
      )
    }, error=function(e) NULL)
  })
  h5$close_all()

  bind_rows(results) |>
    filter(lon >= region$lon_min, lon <= region$lon_max,
           lat >= region$lat_min, lat <= region$lat_max)
}

scbi_raw   <- list.files("data/gedi_l4a_scbi", "\\.h5$", full.names=TRUE) |>
  lapply(extract_l4a, region=scbi) |> bind_rows()

scbi_clean <- scbi_raw |>
  filter(quality == 1, degrade == 0, agbd >= 0, agbd < 1500)

section: Step 4 — Build Airborne LiDAR Reference Biomass
text:
Step 4 — Build Airborne LiDAR Reference Biomass
Neither NEON AOP nor 3DEP provides AGBD directly — they provide canopy height models (CHMs). To make them comparable to GEDI L4A, we apply the same power-law allometric model used in published SCBI biomass inventories.

Allometric model
\[\text{AGBD} = 0.90 \times \text{CHM}^{1.65} \quad [\text{Mg/ha}]\]
This model is calibrated for temperate deciduous forest such that CHM = 32 m → ~250 Mg/ha, consistent with published SCBI mean biomass (~220–280 Mg/ha). The exponent 1.65 reflects the empirical relationship between stand height and biomass across eastern US deciduous forests.


NEON AOP 2019 CHM

library(neonUtilities)

byTileAOP(
  dpID     = "DP3.30015.001",   # Ecosystem structure — CHM
  site     = "SCBI",
  year     = "2019",
  easting  = scbi$utm_e,
  northing = scbi$utm_n,
  buffer   = 400,
  check.size = FALSE,
  savepath = "data/neon_chm_scbi"
)

chm_neon <- list.files("data/neon_chm_scbi", "\\.tif$",
                        recursive=TRUE, full.names=TRUE) |>
  lapply(rast) |> sprc() |> mosaic() |> project("EPSG:4326")



3DEP LiDAR (~2017) CHM

library(httr); library(jsonlite); library(lidR)

tnm_url <- paste0(
  "https://tnmaccess.nationalmap.gov/api/v1/products?",
  "datasets=Lidar+Point+Cloud+%283DEP%29&",
  "bbox=", scbi$lon_min, ",", scbi$lat_min, ",",
           scbi$lon_max, ",", scbi$lat_max,
  "&outputFormat=JSON&max=20"
)
tiles <- fromJSON(content(GET(tnm_url), "text"))

dir.create("data/3dep_scbi", showWarnings=FALSE)
for (url in tiles$items$downloadURL) {
  f <- file.path("data/3dep_scbi", basename(url))
  if (!file.exists(f)) download.file(url, f, mode="wb", quiet=TRUE)
}

ctg      <- readLAScatalog("data/3dep_scbi/")
opt_chunk_buffer(ctg) <- 15
ctg_norm <- normalize_height(ctg, knnidw(k=8, p=2))
chm_3dep <- rasterize_canopy(ctg_norm, res=1,
              algorithm=pitfree(c(0,2,5,10,15,20), c(0,1.5))) |>
  project("EPSG:4326")



Extract CHM at GEDI Footprints and Convert to AGBD

library(exactextractr)

chm_to_agbd <- function(h) pmax(20, 0.90 * h^1.65)

gedi_sf  <- st_as_sf(scbi_clean, coords=c("lon","lat"), crs=4326) |>
  st_transform(32617)
gedi_buf <- st_buffer(gedi_sf, dist=12.5)

scbi_clean$neon_chm  <- exact_extract(
  chm_neon |> project("EPSG:32617"), gedi_buf, fun="mean")

scbi_clean$dep_chm   <- exact_extract(
  chm_3dep |> project("EPSG:32617"), gedi_buf, fun="mean")

scbi_clean <- scbi_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(neon_chm), !is.na(dep_chm),
         neon_chm > 2, dep_chm > 2) |>
  mutate(
    agbd_neon = chm_to_agbd(neon_chm),
    agbd_3dep = chm_to_agbd(dep_chm - 1.0)   # −1 m to account for ~2yr growth offset
  )

The −1 m correction on 3DEP CHM accounts for the ~2-year temporal gap: at SCBI, temperate deciduous forest grows ~0.3–0.5 m/yr in height, so the 2017 acquisition underestimates 2019-era heights by roughly 1 m.

Key findings (40 footprints, 2019–2022):

GEDI L4A AGBD substantially overestimates allometric predictions — by +77.8 Mg/ha vs NEON and +69.2 Mg/ha vs 3DEP. GEDI L4A mean AGBD = 158 Mg/ha, while NEON CHM allometry yields ~80 Mg/ha and 3DEP allometry ~89 Mg/ha for the same footprints. This positive bias likely reflects the GEDI L4A neural-network model being trained on diverse global forest types; the temperate deciduous allometry used here (AGBD = 0.90 × CHM^1.65) may underestimate relative to GEDI’s inference.
Good relative agreement (R² = 0.62–0.63) — despite the absolute offset, GEDI L4A and allometric estimates rank footprints similarly: taller-canopy footprints map to higher AGBD in all three sources.
NEON and 3DEP allometries agree very well (R² = 0.980, RMSE = 12.6 Mg/ha) — the −8.6 Mg/ha NEON vs 3DEP bias is within expected allometric model uncertainty.





GEDI Prediction Interval Width


Each GEDI footprint is provided with a 90% prediction interval (PI). PI width increases with AGBD — taller, denser forest increases model uncertainty because the allometric model has more leverage at higher biomass. Mean PI at SCBI is ~145 Mg/ha (~60% of mean AGBD), consistent with V002 uncertainty bounds reported by Duncanson et al. (2022).




AGBD Distribution — Three Sources


All three sources show distributions consistent with temperate deciduous forest. GEDI L4A (mean ~158 Mg/ha) is substantially higher than the two CHM-allometric estimates (NEON ~80 Mg/ha, 3DEP ~89 Mg/ha). The NEON and 3DEP allometric estimates are tightly clustered (R² = 0.980), confirming that the large GEDI offset is a model-level difference rather than noise. SCBI forest biomass from ground measurements (Anderson-Teixeira et al. 2015) is ~220–280 Mg/ha, suggesting the allometric model used here (AGBD = 0.90 × CHM^1.65) may underestimate field-measured biomass while GEDI L4A provides values closer to inventory estimates.

title: GEDI L4A Above-Ground Biomass at NEON SCBI: Comparison with NEON AOP and 3DEP Allometric Estimates
text:
Key Notes

AGBD uncertainty is large at footprint scale: The mean 90% PI width at SCBI is ~145 Mg/ha. This is intrinsic to the L4A allometric model — do not interpret individual footprint values as precise measurements.
GEDI L4A (mean ~158 Mg/ha) is closer to inventory values (~220–280 Mg/ha) than the allometric estimates (~80–89 Mg/ha): The simple power-law CHM allometry used for comparison underestimates relative to GEDI’s neural-network model trained on global forest inventory plots.
Allometric amplification: Because AGBD ∝ CHM^1.65, a 5 m height bias produces a ~40–70 Mg/ha biomass bias. Height accuracy in L2A directly determines L4A accuracy.
NEON vs 3DEP allometric bias is small (−8.6 Mg/ha, R² = 0.98): The two CHM sources agree very well, confirming that the large GEDI offset is a model-level difference, not a height-data problem.
Always use V002: The V002 allometric models are significantly improved over V001, particularly for broadleaf forests.
Power beams: BEAM0101, BEAM0110, BEAM1000, BEAM1011 yield higher-quality waveforms in dense canopy — include beam as a diagnostic if agreement is unexpectedly poor.

section: Step 2 — Build Canopy Height Model (CHM) from 3DEP
text:
Step 2 — Build Canopy Height Model (CHM) from 3DEP
The CHM = Digital Surface Model (DSM) − Digital Terrain Model (DTM). It gives the height of everything above bare ground — trees, buildings, bridges.

library(lidR)

ctg <- readLAScatalog("data/3dep_laz/")
opt_chunk_buffer(ctg) <- 15        # 15 m buffer to avoid edge artifacts
opt_select(ctg)       <- "xyzr"   # x, y, z, return number

# Step 1: Normalize to height above ground
ctg_norm <- normalize_height(ctg, knnidw(k=8, p=2))

# Step 2: Canopy Height Model (1 m resolution, pitfree algorithm)
chm_1m <- rasterize_canopy(
  ctg_norm, res=1,
  algorithm=pitfree(thresholds=c(0, 2, 5, 10, 15), max_edge=c(0, 1.5))
)

# Step 3: Light smoothing to fill small gaps
chm_1m <- focal(chm_1m, w=matrix(1, 3, 3), fun=mean, na.rm=TRUE)

# Step 4: Aggregate to 30 m for visualization
chm_30m <- aggregate(chm_1m, fact=30, fun=max, na.rm=TRUE)

# Building height model: max return per cell (30 m)
bldg_hm <- rasterize_canopy(ctg_norm, res=30,
                             algorithm=p2r(subcircle=0.15))



The 3DEP CHM shows Central Park’s tree canopy at 15–25 m (green), a dense high-rise corridor in Midtown and Lower Manhattan (yellow–red), and near-zero values on major streets. This raster is the reference for all comparisons below.

Step 3 — Extract 3DEP CHM at GEDI Footprint Locations
For each GEDI footprint (~25 m diameter), we extract the mean 3DEP CHM within a 12.5 m radius buffer — matching the GEDI footprint geometry as closely as possible.

# Load quality-filtered GEDI data (from Urban GEDI post workflow)
nyc_clean <- readRDS("../gedi-urban-nyc/shots_clean.rds")

# Buffer GEDI footprints to ~25 m diameter
gedi_sf <- st_as_sf(nyc_clean, coords=c("lon","lat"), crs=4326) |>
  st_transform(32618)   # UTM zone 18N for buffering in metres

gedi_buf <- st_buffer(gedi_sf, dist=12.5)

# Extract mean 3DEP CHM within each buffer
gedi_sf$dep_chm <- exact_extract(chm_1m |> project("EPSG:32618"),
                                   gedi_buf, fun="mean")

# Back to WGS84
gedi_sf <- st_transform(gedi_sf, 4326)

Building footprints show more moderate positive bias (+4.8 m average). Step 5 — Practical Fusion Strategy
No single source is complete. A practical urban workflow fuses all three:

# Step 1: Use 3DEP CHM as the primary height reference (best accuracy)
# Step 2: For GEDI footprints on buildings, correct systematic bias
bias_model <- lm(rh95 ~ dep_height + I(dep_height^2), data=bldg_shots)
gedi_corrected <- predict(bias_model, newdata=gedi_joined)

# Step 3: Fill OSM gaps with 3DEP building height polygons
bldg_complete <- bldg_poly |>
  mutate(height_final = coalesce(osm_height, dep_height))

# Step 4: For vegetation mapping, prefer 3DEP CHM but use GEDI where
# 3DEP is unavailable (outside CONUS or older vintages)
nyc_veg_height <- gedi_joined |>
  filter(surface_type == "Vegetation") |>
  mutate(height_best = coalesce(dep_chm, rh95))

title: Statistical Modeling
text: Statistical modeling describes the probabilistic relationship between a response variable and one or more predictors through a mathematical framework that explicitly characterizes data-generating processes and uncertainty. Core approaches range from classical linear and generalized linear models (GLMs) to hierarchical mixed-effects models, Bayesian inference, and time-series methods.

title: Statistical Modeling
text:
Basic Mechanisms
Linear and generalized linear models assume that the response is a (possibly transformed) linear function of predictors plus random error drawn from a specified distribution (Gaussian, Poisson, binomial, gamma). Mixed-effects models extend this by partitioning variance into fixed effects (population-level relationships) and random effects (site-, species-, or plot-level deviations), making them well-suited to nested ecological data structures. Bayesian inference frames parameter estimation as updating prior beliefs with observed data via Bayes’ theorem, producing full posterior distributions rather than point estimates. Time-series methods — including autoregressive models, spectral decomposition, and change-point detection algorithms such as LandTrendr and CCDC — characterize temporal trends, seasonality, and abrupt shifts in remote sensing records.

title: Statistical Modeling
text:
Advantages

Interpretability — model coefficients have direct physical or ecological meaning (e.g., sensitivity of NPP to temperature)
Formal uncertainty quantification — confidence intervals and posterior distributions propagate parameter uncertainty into predictions
Well-established theory — decades of methodological literature support robust diagnostics and assumption testing
Efficient with small samples — parametric assumptions reduce the data needed relative to flexible ML approaches
Handles structured data — mixed-effects and hierarchical models naturally accommodate repeated measures, nested designs, and spatial autocorrelation

title: Statistical Modeling
text:
Disadvantages

Distributional assumptions — misspecified error distributions or link functions produce biased inference
Limited nonlinearity — polynomial and spline extensions help, but classical regression struggles with highly complex, high-dimensional response surfaces
Sensitivity to outliers — least-squares estimation is strongly influenced by extreme observations
Collinearity — correlated predictors inflate variance inflation factors and destabilize coefficient estimates
Stationarity assumptions — many time-series methods assume stationary relationships that may not hold under climate non-stationarity

title: Statistical Modeling
text:
Applications in Ecosystem Research

Quantifying climate sensitivity of net primary production (NPP) across models and scenarios
Allometric regression linking tree diameter and height to above-ground biomass
Mixed-effects models for urban cooling intensity as a function of canopy structure across cities
LandTrendr / CCDC for detecting and dating forest disturbance from Landsat time series
Bayesian hierarchical models for integrating multi-source biomass observations with uncertainty

title: Machine Learning
text: Machine learning (ML) algorithms learn predictive mappings from data without being explicitly programmed with domain equations. In ecological and remote sensing research, three broad families are in active use: interpretable / knowledge-guided machine learning, which prioritizes transparency and the integration of domain theory; deep learning, which leverages hierarchical neural architectures for high-dimensional inputs such as imagery and point clouds; and their joint application to 3D LiDAR point cloud processing, where the geometry and density of millions of returns demand specialized architectures.

title: Machine Learning
text:
1 · Interpretable & Knowledge-Guided Machine Learning

Ensemble Tree Methods
Random Forest constructs many decorrelated decision trees via bootstrap sampling and random feature subsets at each split, then averages predictions to achieve strong accuracy alongside built-in variable importance estimates. Gradient boosting methods (XGBoost, LightGBM) build trees sequentially so each tree corrects the residuals of the prior ensemble through gradient descent on the loss function — typically outperforming Random Forest on tabular ecological data with sufficient training samples.



Interpretability Tools — SHAP
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) provides post-hoc interpretability by decomposing each prediction into additive contributions from individual features, grounded in cooperative game theory. For ecological applications this means a Random Forest or XGBoost biomass estimate can be attributed to specific drivers — canopy height, VPD, soil moisture — with directional and magnitude information. SHAP interaction values further reveal how two predictors jointly modulate predictions, enabling physically meaningful analysis of black-box ensembles.



Knowledge-Guided / Physics-Informed ML
Purely data-driven models can violate physical laws (e.g., predicting negative biomass, or NPP that exceeds radiation limits) and fail outside training conditions. Knowledge-guided ML embeds domain constraints directly into the learning process:

Physics-informed loss functions — add penalty terms that penalize violations of energy balance, mass conservation, or known monotonic relationships (e.g., GPP must increase with radiation up to light saturation)
Feature engineering from process understanding — input features are constructed as physically meaningful compound variables (fAPAR × PAR, VPD × stomatal conductance proxy) rather than raw band reflectances
Hybrid PBM–ML models — a process-based model provides baseline predictions; ML corrects residuals arising from structural error or missing processes; the combined output respects physical bounds while capturing complex patterns
Transfer learning with domain adaptation — pre-trained models are fine-tuned on target ecosystems with physical consistency constraints, reducing the labeled data requirement

These approaches improve generalization to novel climate or land-cover conditions where purely empirical models degrade.



Advantages

Captures complex nonlinearity — no assumption of linearity, monotonicity, or specific functional form
Handles high-dimensional inputs — spectral bands, LiDAR metrics, topographic derivatives, and climate variables can all enter jointly
Built-in variable importance — tree ensembles naturally rank predictor relevance; SHAP provides directional attribution
Physically consistent outputs — knowledge-guided constraints prevent ecologically implausible predictions
Scalable — scales to millions of training samples; GPU-accelerated variants scale further




Disadvantages

Poor extrapolation without constraints — purely data-driven models are unreliable outside the feature space of training data
Overfitting — without careful spatial cross-validation, accuracy metrics are inflated by spatial autocorrelation
No inherent uncertainty — point predictions require additional frameworks (quantile regression forests, conformal prediction) for intervals
Stationarity assumption — models trained on current conditions may fail under non-stationary climate regimes

title: Machine Learning
text:
2 · Deep Learning
Deep learning (DL) uses multi-layer neural networks to learn hierarchical feature representations directly from raw data, bypassing hand-crafted feature engineering. For remote sensing and ecological research, four architectures dominate.


Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
CNNs apply learned spatial filters (kernels) across image grids in successive layers, progressively extracting local-to-global features. In remote sensing they are the standard architecture for land cover classification, tree crown delineation, and urban mapping from multispectral or hyperspectral raster data. Encoder–decoder variants (U-Net, DeepLab) produce pixel-wise segmentation outputs used for canopy and impervious surface mapping.



Recurrent Networks & Transformers for Time Series
LSTMs and GRUs capture temporal dependencies in satellite time-series (e.g., Landsat/Sentinel-2 EVI or LAI stacks) for phenology extraction, disturbance detection, and GPP estimation. Vision Transformers (ViT) and temporal attention mechanisms increasingly replace recurrent layers, using self-attention to weight the relative importance of observations across time and space — including irregular acquisition intervals from cloud masking.



Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)
GNNs operate on irregular graph-structured data rather than grids, making them naturally suited to ecological networks (species interaction graphs, plot connectivity) and, increasingly, to point cloud processing where each return is a node with spatial edges to neighbors.



Advantages

State-of-the-art accuracy on image classification, segmentation, and time-series tasks
Automatic feature learning — no manual spectral index or texture feature engineering
Flexible architectures — can be adapted to multi-modal inputs (imagery + LiDAR + SAR)
Transfer learning — ImageNet- or Satlas-pretrained backbones require far less labeled ecological data for fine-tuning




Disadvantages

Data hungry — requires large labeled datasets that are expensive to produce in remote sensing
Computationally intensive — GPU clusters required for training at scale
Black-box behavior — interpretability requires additional tools (GradCAM, attention visualization)
Spatial autocorrelation risk — geographic train/test splits essential to avoid inflated accuracy

title: Machine Learning
section: 3 · Machine Learning for LiDAR Point Cloud Processing
text:
3 · Machine Learning for LiDAR Point Cloud Processing
Airborne, spaceborne, and terrestrial LiDAR systems produce point clouds — unordered sets of 3D returns (x, y, z) with optional intensity and return-number attributes. Extracting ecologically and structurally meaningful information from these clouds requires algorithms that handle irregular spatial sampling, variable density, and occlusion. ML and DL have transformed point cloud analysis across four core tasks.


Point Cloud Classification & Semantic Segmentation
Assigning each return a semantic label (ground, low/medium/high vegetation, building, noise) is the foundational step for any downstream analysis. Classical approaches (height-above-ground thresholds, normalized cut clustering) have been largely replaced by:

PointNet / PointNet++ — pioneer architectures that process raw (x, y, z) point sets directly using shared MLP layers and local neighborhood aggregation (set abstraction), learning per-point and global features without voxelization. Widely applied to classify airborne LiDAR returns into ground, shrub, tree, and structure classes.
RandLA-Net — efficient random sampling with local feature aggregation, enabling semantic segmentation of large outdoor scenes with tens of millions of points at low memory cost.
KPConv (Kernel Point Convolution) — defines convolution kernels in 3D space anchored at kernel points, enabling spatially consistent feature learning without a regular grid; highly accurate for ALS forest classification.




Individual Tree Detection & Crown Segmentation

3D Instance Segmentation — models such as PointGroup, HAIS, and Mask3D extend semantic segmentation to individual instance delineation, separating adjacent tree crowns in dense forest canopy point clouds.
Deep Learning–Enhanced Watershed / Region Growing — CNN-predicted seed points or crown probability maps guide classical watershed segmentation on normalized canopy height models (nCHMs), combining the interpretability of raster-based methods with DL accuracy.
RANSAC + GNN — trunk detection via RANSAC cylinder fitting, followed by GNN-based crown-to-trunk association for individual tree isolation in terrestrial LiDAR (TLS) scenes.




Biomass & Structural Attribute Estimation
Once point clouds are segmented, ML models translate 3D structural metrics into forest inventory attributes:







Target attribute
Common ML approach




Above-ground biomass (AGB)
Random Forest / XGBoost from height percentiles, canopy cover, density metrics


Tree height & crown volume
Direct measurement from segmented point cloud; DL refinement for overlapping crowns


Leaf area index (LAI)
Gap fraction inversion from TLS hemispherical profiles; RF from ALS density layers


Stem diameter (DBH)
RANSAC cylinder fitting on TLS trunk returns; CNN regression on cross-sectional slices


Wood volume
Quantitative Structure Models (QSM: TreeQSM, AdQSM) reconstructing branching geometry






Change Detection & Forest Disturbance Mapping
Multi-temporal ALS or repeat GEDI acquisitions enable 3D change detection beyond what 2D imagery can resolve:

Siamese PointNet and 3D U-Net change detection networks take paired pre/post point clouds as dual-branch inputs and predict per-point change labels (mortality, growth, windthrow, harvest)
Height difference rasters + RF classification — differencing normalized canopy height models between epochs, then classifying change magnitude and spatial pattern with Random Forest to distinguish disturbance type (fire scorch vs. mechanical harvest vs. wind damage)
GEDI L2A/L4A time series — footprint-level RH metrics (RH50, RH98) tracked across repeat acquisitions with anomaly detection (isolation forest, LSTM autoencoder) to flag canopy loss events at near-global scale

title: Methods — Introduction
text: This section outlines the methodological framework underlying my research. Four complementary approaches are combined to characterize ecosystem structure and function, quantify environmental drivers, and project future ecosystem dynamics under climate change. Each method has distinct mechanisms, strengths, and limitations; their integration provides analytical robustness that no single approach can achieve alone.

title: Methods — Introduction
text:
Integrative Framework
No single method is sufficient for understanding ecosystem dynamics under climate change. My research combines these approaches in a layered framework:

Statistical modeling establishes baseline empirical relationships and characterizes variability in observational records
Machine learning scales those relationships spatially across large domains using multi-source remote sensing data
Causal inference distinguishes genuine driver effects from spurious correlations in observational data
Process-based models provide mechanistic constraints for extrapolation to future climate conditions beyond the observational record







Note



Reproducible code implementing these methods is available in the Blog/Notes section and linked from individual Research projects.

title: Key Assumptions
text: Every analytical method rests on assumptions that define the conditions under which its results are valid. Being explicit about these assumptions is not a limitation — it is a prerequisite for rigorous, reproducible science. The assumptions below are organized by the research contexts in which they most commonly arise across forest biomass estimation, urban green space cooling, and ecosystem responses to climate extremes.

title: Key Assumptions
text:
Statistical & Machine Learning Assumptions

Stationarity — relationships between predictors (e.g., spectral features, LiDAR metrics) and response variables (AGB, LST) are assumed stable across space and time; violated when training in one biome and predicting in another
Representativeness of training data — field plots or GEDI footprints used as labels are assumed to be spatially and structurally representative of the broader landscape
Spatial independence — most ML models assume training and test samples are independent; in practice, spatial autocorrelation inflates accuracy if not handled with spatial cross-validation
Error-in-variables — field AGB measurements used as ground truth carry allometric model uncertainty, which is rarely propagated into the final product uncertainty

title: Key Assumptions
text:
Remote Sensing & Data Assumptions

Radiometric consistency — multi-temporal Landsat/Sentinel composites assume atmospheric correction removes inter-scene differences; residual BRDF effects can bias spectral indices
GEDI footprint representativeness — GEDI samples ~25 m footprints; gridded products (L4B) assume these footprints statistically represent the surrounding 1 km cell
Allometric generality — biomass allometric equations (height → AGB) developed in one region are applied globally, assuming structural similarity across forests
LiDAR height = biomass proxy — canopy height metrics (RH98, top-of-canopy height) correlate with AGB, but the relationship varies by wood density, species composition, and stand structure

title: Key Assumptions
text:
Causal & Process-Based Assumptions

Temporal precedence — in climate–NPP studies, climate drivers are assumed to precede and cause ecosystem responses, not the reverse (violated under strong vegetation–climate feedbacks)
No unmeasured confounding — attribution of NPP variability to temperature or drought requires that other co-varying drivers (CO₂, nitrogen deposition, land use) are either measured or assumed negligible
Process stationarity in PBMs — DGVMs assume fixed plant functional type parameters (Vcmax, allocation fractions) that do not adapt over the simulation period; violated under rapid climate change or species migration
Steady-state carbon balance — many biomass estimation studies assume old-growth forests are near carbon equilibrium; violated in post-disturbance recovering stands

title: Key Assumptions
text:
Urban Cooling Assumptions

Uniform atmospheric demand — the Penman–Monteith / TRM framework assumes spatially uniform VPD and reference ET conditions across a city; urban heterogeneity in humidity and wind speed violates this
Independent cooling pathways — studies that estimate shading and ET cooling separately often assume additivity, but shading reduces ET by lowering leaf temperature, creating a negative interaction
LST as air temperature proxy — land surface temperature (Landsat, ECOSTRESS) is used as a proxy for human thermal comfort, but the LST–Tair relationship varies strongly with surface type and wind speed

title: Optical Remote Sensing Datasets
text: Multispectral and hyperspectral satellite imagery from open-access programs widely used in land cover mapping, vegetation monitoring, and environmental change detection.

title: Optical Remote Sensing Datasets
text:
Landsat — USGS / NASA
Landsat is the longest-running Earth observation satellite program, continuously collecting multispectral imagery since 1972. Operated jointly by USGS and NASA, the program provides a free and open archive essential for long-term land surface change analysis.
Current sensors: Landsat 8 OLI/TIRS · Landsat 9 OLI-2/TIRS-2 Spatial resolution: 30 m (multispectral) · 15 m (panchromatic) · 100 m (thermal) Temporal resolution: 16-day revisit per satellite (~8 days combined) Spectral bands: Coastal/aerosol, Blue, Green, Red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, Panchromatic, Thermal Coverage: Global, continuous since 1972 Key applications: Land cover change, deforestation, urban expansion, agricultural monitoring, wildfire burn severity, surface temperature






Note



Landsat data are freely available through USGS EarthExplorer and Google Earth Engine.

title: Optical Remote Sensing Datasets
text:
Sentinel-2 — ESA Copernicus
Sentinel-2 is a high-resolution multispectral mission from the European Space Agency (ESA) under the Copernicus Earth Observation Programme. Its combination of high spatial resolution, frequent revisit time, and free data access has made it one of the most widely used satellites in vegetation and land surface research.
Sensors: MultiSpectral Instrument (MSI) — Sentinel-2A and Sentinel-2B Spatial resolution: 10 m (B2, B3, B4, B8) · 20 m (B5, B6, B7, B8A, B11, B12) · 60 m (B1, B9, B10) Temporal resolution: ~5-day revisit (combined twin satellites) Spectral bands: 13 bands from visible to SWIR, including red-edge bands for vegetation analysis Coverage: Global land surface Key applications: Forest canopy health, LAI estimation, crop monitoring, urban green space mapping, water body detection






Note



Sentinel-2 data are freely available through the Copernicus Data Space and Google Earth Engine.

title: Optical Remote Sensing Datasets
text:
HLS — Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (NASA)
HLS is a NASA-produced data product that harmonizes observations from the Landsat 8/9 OLI and Sentinel-2A/B MSI sensors into a consistent surface reflectance time series. By cross-calibrating the two satellite programs, HLS provides a near-seamless 30 m multispectral record with a ~2–3 day effective revisit, significantly reducing the data gaps introduced by cloud cover.
Agency: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Sensors: Landsat 8 OLI · Landsat 9 OLI-2 · Sentinel-2A MSI · Sentinel-2B MSI (harmonized jointly) Spatial resolution: 30 m Temporal resolution: ~2–3 day effective revisit (combined four sensors) Spectral bands: 10 common bands (Coastal/Aerosol, Blue, Green, Red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2, Cirrus, SWIR-S2 equivalent) consistently cross-calibrated across sensors Products: - HLSL30 — Landsat-derived surface reflectance (30 m) - HLSS30 — Sentinel-2-derived surface reflectance (30 m, resampled) Coverage: Global land, from 2013 (Landsat 8) onward Key applications: Dense time-series vegetation phenology, crop monitoring, forest disturbance detection, intra-seasonal land cover change, gap-filling cloud-contaminated records






Tip



HLS is especially powerful for detecting short-duration events (e.g., crop harvest, defoliation outbreaks, wildfire) that require sub-weekly sampling, which neither Landsat nor Sentinel-2 alone can reliably provide.








Note



HLS data are freely available through NASA EarthData (HLSL30 and HLSS30 collections) and Google Earth Engine (NASA/HLS).

title: Optical Remote Sensing Datasets
section: ECOSTRESS — ECOsystem Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment on Space Station (NASA / JPL)
text:
ECOSTRESS — ECOsystem Spaceborne Thermal Radiometer Experiment on Space Station (NASA / JPL)
ECOSTRESS is a NASA thermal infrared multispectral radiometer mounted on the International Space Station (ISS), designed to measure land surface temperature (LST) and evapotranspiration (ET) at fine spatial resolution (~70 m). Unlike sun-synchronous satellites that always acquire data at the same local time, ECOSTRESS benefits from the ISS’s precessing orbit — sampling a given location at varying times of day across repeated overpasses, enabling the capture of diurnal LST and ET cycles invisible to Landsat or Sentinel-based thermal products. This makes it uniquely suited for studying plant water stress responses, urban heat island dynamics, and irrigation water use across diverse ecosystems.
Agency: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — Principal Investigators: Josh Fisher, Simon Hook Platform: International Space Station (ISS), orbit inclination ~51.6° Launch: June 2018 Sensor: 5-band thermal infrared radiometer (TIR), 8.0–12.0 μm Spatial resolution: ~70 m (resampled from native ~38 m × 69 m instantaneous field of view) Temporal resolution: Irregular (~4-day average revisit); ISS precession provides diurnal sampling diversity Coverage: ±51.6° latitude (ISS orbital limit) Key data products:







Product
Description




ECO2LSTE
Land Surface Temperature & Emissivity (70 m)


ECO3ETPTJPL
Evapotranspiration — PT-JPL model (70 m)


ECO3ETALEXI
ET — Atmosphere-Land Exchange Inverse (ALEXI) model


ECO4ESIPTJPL
Evaporative Stress Index (ESI) — plant water stress indicator


ECO4WUE
Water Use Efficiency (GPP / ET)



Key applications: - Urban heat island analysis — 70 m LST resolves individual city blocks, parks, and street canyons far better than Landsat’s 100 m thermal band; ideal for quantifying the cooling effect of urban green space - Drought and plant water stress — Evaporative Stress Index (ESI) detects early-onset drought stress before visible spectral changes occur - Agricultural ET and irrigation mapping — field-scale ET products compatible with crop water use models - Ecosystem carbon–water coupling — Water Use Efficiency (WUE) links carbon assimilation to transpiration demand across biomes






Tip



ECOSTRESS’s ~70 m thermal resolution is the finest available from a spaceborne platform, making it the preferred dataset for city-scale LST studies where Landsat’s 100 m thermal product cannot resolve the spatial heterogeneity of urban green space patches, impervious surfaces, and building rooftops.








Note



ECOSTRESS data are freely available through NASA EarthData / LP DAAC and Google Earth Engine (NASA/ECOSTRESS/ETinst). The full product suite is documented at the ECOSTRESS mission page.

title: Optical Remote Sensing Datasets
text:
MODIS — NASA Terra & Aqua
MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) is a key instrument aboard NASA’s Terra and Aqua satellites. While its spatial resolution is coarser than Landsat or Sentinel-2, its near-daily global coverage and long record (since 1999) make it indispensable for large-scale vegetation dynamics, land surface temperature, and fire monitoring.
Agency: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Sensors: MODIS aboard Terra (EOS AM-1) and Aqua (EOS PM-1) Spatial resolution: 250 m (bands 1–2) · 500 m (bands 3–7) · 1000 m (bands 8–36) Temporal resolution: Daily global coverage (1–2 days revisit) Spectral bands: 36 bands from visible to thermal infrared (0.4–14.4 μm) Record length: Terra since February 2000 · Aqua since July 2002 Key products: - MOD13 / MYD13 — Vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI) at 250 m / 500 m / 1 km - MOD15 — Leaf Area Index (LAI) and FPAR - MOD17 — Gross/Net Primary Production (GPP/NPP) - MOD44B — Vegetation continuous fields (tree cover, non-tree, bare ground) - MCD64A1 — Monthly burned area - MOD11 — Land surface temperature and emissivity Key applications: Global vegetation phenology, drought monitoring, wildfire detection, land cover classification, carbon flux estimation, urban heat islands






Note



MODIS data are freely available through NASA EarthData and Google Earth Engine.

title: Optical Remote Sensing Datasets
section: VIIRS — Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (NOAA / NASA)
text:
VIIRS — Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (NOAA / NASA)
VIIRS is the primary visible-to-thermal sensor aboard the Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 satellites. It is the operational successor to MODIS, offering improved radiometric calibration, a wider swath, and a dedicated day-night band (DNB) that enables detection of city lights, gas flares, and fires at night. Its near-daily global coverage makes it a cornerstone dataset for large-scale land and ocean monitoring.
Agency: NOAA / NASA Satellites: Suomi-NPP (2011–present) · NOAA-20 / JPSS-1 (2017–present) · NOAA-21 / JPSS-2 (2022–present) Spatial resolution: 375 m (I-bands, visible/NIR/SWIR/TIR) · 750 m (M-bands, moderate resolution) · ~750 m (DNB) Temporal resolution: ~1-day global revisit Spectral bands: 22 bands from visible (0.41 μm) to longwave thermal infrared (12.5 μm), including a dedicated Day-Night Band (DNB) Key products: - VNP13 — Vegetation indices (NDVI, EVI) at 500 m - VNP09 — Daily surface reflectance - VNP46 — Black Marble nighttime lights - VNP14 — Active fire and thermal anomalies - VJ102IMG — Calibrated top-of-atmosphere radiance (I-bands) Key applications: Nighttime light mapping, active fire detection, vegetation phenology, snow and ice extent, sea surface temperature, aerosol optical depth






Note



VIIRS data are freely available through NASA EarthData and Google Earth Engine. The Black Marble (VNP46) nighttime lights product is also accessible via the NASA Black Marble website.

title: Optical Remote Sensing Datasets
section: GOES — Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (NOAA / NASA)
text:
GOES — Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (NOAA / NASA)
GOES (GOES-16, GOES-17, GOES-18) is NOAA’s geostationary Earth observation system covering the Western Hemisphere. Unlike polar-orbiting sensors, GOES provides nearly continuous observations of a fixed region — as frequently as every 30 seconds during rapid-scan events — making it uniquely suited for near-real-time monitoring of weather, wildfires, and vegetation stress at continental scale.
Agency: NOAA / NASA Satellites: GOES-16 (East, 75.2°W) · GOES-18 (West, 137.2°W) Sensor: ABI — Advanced Baseline Imager Spatial resolution: 0.5 km (visible Band 2) · 1 km (near-IR bands) · 2 km (IR bands) Temporal resolution: Full-disk scan every 10–15 minutes; CONUS sector every 5 minutes; mesoscale every 30–60 seconds Spectral bands: 16 bands from visible (0.47 μm) to longwave IR (13.3 μm) Key products: Cloud cover, fire detection, aerosol optical depth, land surface temperature, vegetation index, lightning mapper (GLM), sea surface temperature Key applications: Wildfire detection and progression, severe weather monitoring, land surface temperature, near-real-time drought assessment, atmospheric water vapor






Note



GOES-ABI data are freely available through NOAA’s AWS S3 bucket (real-time), NOAA CLASS (archive), and Google Earth Engine (NOAA/GOES).

title: Optical Remote Sensing Datasets
text:
NAIP — National Agriculture Imagery Program (USDA)
NAIP (National Agriculture Imagery Program) is a high-resolution aerial imagery program operated by the USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA). It acquires leaf-on orthorectified imagery across the contiguous United States (CONUS) during agricultural growing seasons, making it one of the highest-resolution freely available datasets for land surface analysis in the US.
Agency: USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) Spatial resolution: 1 m (standard) · 0.6 m (select states and years) Temporal resolution: State-level acquisition cycles, typically every 2–3 years per state Spectral bands: Red, Green, Blue (RGB) · Near-Infrared (NIR) added since 2007; some products include a 5th band (Red Edge, select years) Coverage: Contiguous United States (CONUS); acquired during peak growing season (leaf-on conditions) Format: Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG); also available as tiled web services Key applications: Land cover and land use mapping, crop type identification, urban tree canopy assessment, riparian vegetation monitoring, change detection at local scale, training data for machine learning models






Tip



Because NAIP is acquired leaf-on and at ~1 m resolution, it is widely used as high-resolution ground truth or training data for coarser satellite products (Landsat, Sentinel-2). NDVI derived from NAIP’s NIR band can resolve individual tree crowns.








Note



NAIP imagery is freely available through USGS EarthExplorer, USDA Box, and Google Earth Engine (USDA/NAIP/DOQQ).

title: Datasets — Introduction
text: Modern ecological and environmental research requires observations spanning multiple platforms, spatial resolutions, and temporal depths. No single sensor or dataset provides a complete picture of ecosystem structure, function, and change — the strength of contemporary analysis lies in integrating complementary data streams that together constrain what no individual source can resolve alone.

title: Datasets — Introduction
text:
Why Multi-Source Data Integration?
Ecosystems operate across a vast range of scales: individual tree crowns at sub-meter resolution, forest stands at tens of meters, landscapes at kilometers, and biomes at continental to global extents. Similarly, ecological processes unfold across timescales from diurnal photosynthetic cycles to century-long successional dynamics. A single sensor designed for one scale inevitably sacrifices information at others.
Multi-source data integration addresses this by combining:

High spatial resolution measurements (airborne LiDAR, NAIP) for fine-scale structural detail
High temporal frequency observations (MODIS, GOES, VIIRS) for phenological and disturbance dynamics
Long historical archives (Landsat since 1972, FIA since the 1930s) for decadal trend detection
Global coverage (GEDI, ICESat-2, Sentinel missions) for analyses beyond locally surveyed regions
Ground truth (field inventory plots, eddy covariance towers) for model calibration and validation

When combined, these sources enable analyses that are simultaneously spatially explicit, temporally consistent, and ecologically interpretable.

title: Datasets — Introduction
text:
Cross-Scale Validation Framework
A core principle underlying the use of these datasets is cross-scale validation: measurements from one platform are used to evaluate or calibrate estimates from another. Common validation chains include:

Field plots → Airborne LiDAR → Spaceborne LiDAR (GEDI) → Global maps for above-ground biomass
Eddy covariance towers (FLUXNET) → MODIS/Sentinel-2 → Global GPP products for carbon flux
Airborne LiDAR (NEON AOP) → ICESat-2/GEDI footprints → Global canopy height for forest structure

Each transition up the scale ladder introduces assumptions and uncertainties; a transparent multi-source framework makes those assumptions explicit and testable.

title: Datasets — Introduction
text:
Data Access Philosophy
All datasets described on this site are freely and openly accessible to the research community. Where possible, access links point to:

Google Earth Engine — for cloud-based analysis without local download
NASA EarthData / USGS EarthExplorer — for full-resolution archive access
NEON / FIA data portals — for standardized ecological field data
Zenodo / PANGAEA — for community-deposited research datasets

Open data accelerates science by enabling reproducibility, cross-study comparisons, and analyses in data-limited regions where ground-based observations are scarce.
