title: Evaluation Metrics
text: Quantitative metrics are the language through which model performance, dataset quality, and trend significance are communicated. Choosing the right metric — and understanding what it does and does not capture — is as important as the model itself. This page documents the metrics most commonly used across forest biomass estimation, urban cooling analysis, and ecosystem response studies.

title: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Goodness-of-Fit Metrics


R² — Coefficient of Determination
\[R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}\]
Interpretation: The proportion of variance in the observed values \(y_i\) explained by the model predictions \(\hat{y}_i\). Ranges from \(-\infty\) to 1; a value of 1 indicates perfect prediction, 0 indicates the model performs no better than the mean, and negative values indicate the model is worse than predicting the mean.
Common use: Biomass model fit, LST prediction accuracy, NPP–climate regression.
Pitfalls: - A high R² does not guarantee low prediction error — the model may explain variance but still have large systematic offsets - R² increases monotonically as predictors are added; use adjusted R² for comparing models of different complexity - R² is sensitive to the range of \(y\): artificially wide ranges inflate R²






Tip



In remote sensing regression (e.g., GEDI AGB vs. field AGB), R² is almost always reported alongside RMSE — R² quantifies explanatory power, RMSE quantifies prediction error in the original units.





r and r² — Pearson Correlation Coefficient
\[r = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2 \cdot \sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2}}\]
Interpretation: \(r\) measures the linear association between two variables, ranging from −1 (perfect negative) to +1 (perfect positive). \(r^2\) is the square of the Pearson correlation — it equals R² only when the regression passes through the origin and is fit by OLS without an intercept. In general, \(r^2 \neq R^2\).
Key distinction from R²: | Metric | What it measures | Range | |——–|—————–|——-| | \(r\) | Strength and direction of linear association | −1 to 1 | | \(r^2\) | Proportion of shared variance (symmetric) | 0 to 1 | | \(R^2\) | Proportion of \(y\) variance explained by the model (asymmetric) | \(-\infty\) to 1 |
Common use: Climate–NPP relationships, canopy height vs. AGB, LST vs. canopy cover correlations.
Pitfalls: - \(r\) detects only linear association; nonlinear relationships can yield \(r \approx 0\) even when a strong relationship exists - Sensitive to outliers — a single extreme point can substantially inflate \(r\) - For non-normal data, use Spearman’s \(\rho\) (rank correlation) instead

title: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Error Metrics


RMSE — Root Mean Square Error
\[\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2}\]
Interpretation: The square root of the average squared residual — expressed in the same units as \(y\). RMSE penalizes large errors more heavily than small ones due to the squaring, making it sensitive to outliers.
Common use: AGB prediction error (Mg ha⁻¹), LST prediction error (°C), ET estimation error (mm/day).
Pitfalls: - Not scale-free — cannot compare RMSE across datasets with different units or ranges; use rRMSE instead - Dominated by large errors, which may or may not be ecologically meaningful - Does not reveal the direction of error (use MBE or Bias for that)



rRMSE — Relative RMSE
\[\text{rRMSE} = \frac{\text{RMSE}}{\bar{y}} \times 100\%\]
Interpretation: RMSE expressed as a percentage of the mean observed value. Scale-free, enabling comparison across datasets, sensors, or biomes.
Common use: Comparing biomass estimation accuracy across tropical vs. boreal forests; benchmarking different sensor combinations.
Typical thresholds (AGB remote sensing): - rRMSE < 20% — excellent - rRMSE 20–40% — acceptable - rRMSE > 40% — poor



MAE — Mean Absolute Error
\[\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\hat{y}_i - y_i|\]
Interpretation: The average absolute residual in the original units of \(y\). Unlike RMSE, MAE weights all errors equally regardless of magnitude, making it more robust to outliers.
When to prefer MAE over RMSE: - When large errors should not be disproportionately penalized - When the error distribution is heavy-tailed (e.g., biomass in high-density old-growth stands) - When communicating results to non-technical audiences (more interpretable)
Common use: Canopy height error, NPP prediction error, urban LST estimation.



Bias (%) — Systematic Prediction Offset
\[\text{Bias (\%)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\hat{y}_i - y_i}{y_i} \times 100\%\]
Interpretation: The average relative over- or under-prediction as a percentage of the observed value. A positive bias means the model systematically overestimates; negative means underestimation.
Why it matters: RMSE and MAE measure scatter around the 1:1 line but cannot distinguish systematic bias from random error. A model can have low RMSE yet a large consistent bias.
Common use: - AGB products tend to underestimate in high-biomass tropical forests (saturation bias) - LST products may show cold or warm biases in urban canyon geometries - DGVM NPP may exhibit systematic overestimation in drought years






Tip



Always report Bias alongside RMSE. Low RMSE + low Bias together indicate both high precision and high accuracy. Low RMSE + high Bias indicates a well-correlated but systematically shifted model.





MBE — Mean Bias Error
\[\text{MBE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat{y}_i - y_i)\]
Interpretation: The average signed residual in the original units. Positive MBE = model overestimates on average; negative = underestimates. Unlike Bias (%), MBE is expressed in the units of \(y\).
Relationship to other metrics:
\[\text{RMSE}^2 = \text{MBE}^2 + \sigma_\varepsilon^2\]
where \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\) is the variance of residuals. This decomposition separates systematic bias from random scatter — useful for diagnosing model errors.



MAPE — Mean Absolute Percentage Error
\[\text{MAPE} = \frac{100\%}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{y_i}\right|\]
Interpretation: Scale-free version of MAE expressed as a percentage. Widely used in forecasting and ecosystem modeling.
Pitfall: Undefined or unstable when \(y_i \approx 0\) — problematic for sparse biomass areas, bare soil, or near-zero NPP in semi-arid regions. Use rRMSE or MAE in those cases.

title: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Model Efficiency Metrics


NSE — Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency
\[\text{NSE} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \bar{y})^2}\]
Interpretation: Dimensionless index (−∞ to 1) widely used in hydrology and ecosystem modeling. NSE = 1 is perfect; NSE = 0 means the model is no better than the observed mean; NSE < 0 means the mean is a better predictor than the model.
Common use: Evaluating DGVM-simulated GPP, ET, and runoff against eddy covariance or streamflow observations; validating process-based urban ET models.
Key relationship: NSE is identical to R² when computed between observed and simulated values from regression through the origin — but for general predictions NSE ≠ R².



IoA — Index of Agreement
\[\text{IoA} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(|\hat{y}_i - \bar{y}| + |y_i - \bar{y}|)^2}\]
Interpretation: Ranges from 0 to 1. Unlike NSE, IoA is bounded below by 0, making it less sensitive to extreme over/underestimation. Values > 0.8 generally indicate good model–observation agreement.
Common use: Process-based model evaluation (DGVMs, urban energy balance models), satellite LST vs. ground measurement comparison.

title: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Trend Metrics


Linear Trend — OLS Slope
\[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(t - \bar{t})(y_t - \bar{y})}{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(t - \bar{t})^2}\]
Interpretation: The ordinary least squares slope of \(y\) on time \(t\), expressed in units of \(y\) per year. Simple, widely used, but sensitive to outliers and non-stationarity.
Common use: Long-term NPP trends from MODIS MOD17, LST warming trends in urban areas, AGB change rates from multi-year LiDAR.
Pitfall: Assumes normally distributed residuals and stationarity. Use Mann-Kendall for non-parametric trend detection when these assumptions are violated.



Mann-Kendall Test — Non-Parametric Trend
The Mann-Kendall test evaluates whether a monotonic upward or downward trend exists in a time series without assuming normality.
Test statistic: \[S = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\sum_{j=i+1}^{n} \text{sgn}(y_j - y_i)\]
where \(\text{sgn}(\cdot)\) is the sign function (+1, 0, −1).
Interpretation: \(S > 0\) suggests an upward trend; \(S < 0\) a downward trend. Statistical significance is assessed via the standardized \(Z\) statistic.
Sen’s Slope — the median of all pairwise slopes \(\frac{y_j - y_i}{j - i}\) — is reported alongside the Mann-Kendall \(p\)-value as a robust trend magnitude estimate.
Common use: - Detecting significant NPP trends in Central Asia despite high interannual variability - Identifying long-term LST warming trends in cities - Forest biomass change detection in repeat LiDAR surveys






Tip



Use Mann-Kendall + Sen’s Slope together: Mann-Kendall provides the significance test, Sen’s Slope provides the magnitude. Both are robust to non-normality and are the standard in ecological trend analysis.

title: Evaluation Metrics
text:
Validation & Model Selection


Cross-Validation Metrics
k-fold cross-validation partitions the dataset into \(k\) folds, training on \(k-1\) and testing on the held-out fold, repeating \(k\) times. The reported RMSE, MAE, and R² are averaged across folds.
Spatial cross-validation — critical in remote sensing — ensures training and test sets are spatially separated to prevent spatial autocorrelation from inflating accuracy. Methods include: - Spatial block CV — geographic blocking by grid cells or regions - Buffered leave-one-out CV (BLOO-CV) — excludes a spatial buffer around each test point - Stratified CV by biome or land cover — ensures representation of all ecosystem types






Important



Standard random k-fold CV applied to spatially autocorrelated remote sensing data can overestimate R² by 0.1–0.3 and underestimate RMSE by 20–40%. Always use spatial CV for LiDAR-based AGB and satellite-derived LST models.





Overfitting Detection
Overfitting occurs when a model captures noise in the training data rather than the underlying signal — yielding low training error but high generalisation error. It is one of the most consequential failure modes in remote sensing regression, where field samples are scarce relative to the number of candidate predictors.

1. Bias-Variance Tradeoff
The expected prediction error of any model decomposes as:
\[\text{MSE}(\hat{f}) = \underbrace{\left[\text{Bias}(\hat{f})\right]^2}_{\text{systematic error}} + \underbrace{\text{Var}(\hat{f})}_{\text{estimation noise}} + \underbrace{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}_{\text{irreducible noise}}\]









Regime
Bias
Variance
Interpretation




Underfitting
High
Low
Model too simple; misses real patterns


Well-generalised
Low
Low
Ideal — train ≈ test performance


Overfitting
Low
High
Model memorises training noise; test error explodes



Model complexity (tree depth, number of features, polynomial degree) increases variance and decreases bias. The optimal complexity minimises their sum.


2. Train–Test Performance Gap
The most direct overfitting diagnostic: compare metrics on held-out data to metrics on training data.
\[\Delta R^2 = R^2_{\text{train}} - R^2_{\text{test}}, \qquad \Delta\text{RMSE} = \text{RMSE}_{\text{test}} - \text{RMSE}_{\text{train}}\]
Rules of thumb for AGB / LST regression:








\(\Delta R^2\)
\(\text{RMSE}_{\text{test}} / \text{RMSE}_{\text{train}}\)
Diagnosis




< 0.05
< 1.15
Acceptable generalisation


0.05–0.15
1.15–1.40
Mild overfitting — consider regularisation or fewer features


> 0.15
> 1.40
Severe overfitting — model is memorising training data









Important



Always report both training and test metrics in publications. Reporting only training R² conceals overfitting and inflates the perceived quality of the model.




3. Learning Curves
A learning curve plots training and validation error (e.g., RMSE) as a function of training sample size \(n\). It separates two fundamentally different failure modes:

High variance (overfitting): training RMSE is low; validation RMSE is high; the gap does not close as \(n\) grows — more data is needed.
High bias (underfitting): both training and validation RMSE converge at a high error level — the model family is too simple.

In AGB remote sensing, learning curves are particularly informative for diagnosing whether additional field plots would substantially reduce prediction error or whether the bottleneck is model architecture.


4. Regularisation
Regularisation constrains model complexity by adding a penalty on parameter magnitudes to the loss function.
Lasso (L1): \[\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \frac{1}{n}\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|\]
Lasso drives some \(\beta_j\) exactly to zero — effectively performing feature selection. Useful when most predictors are irrelevant (e.g., hundreds of spectral bands for AGB prediction).
Ridge (L2): \[\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \frac{1}{n}\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2\]
Ridge shrinks all coefficients but retains all features. Handles multicollinearity well — important for optical remote sensing where spectral bands are highly correlated.
ElasticNet (L1 + L2 combined): \[\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \frac{1}{n}\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^2 + \lambda_1\sum_{j}|\beta_j| + \lambda_2\sum_{j}\beta_j^2\]
Balances sparsity (Lasso) and stability (Ridge). The hyperparameter \(\lambda\) (or \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2\)) is selected via cross-validated RMSE.
For tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost), regularisation is implicit in hyperparameters:







Parameter
Effect on overfitting




max_depth (XGBoost)
Deeper trees → higher variance


min_samples_leaf (RF)
Higher → smoother decision boundary


subsample, colsample_bytree (XGBoost)
Stochastic sampling reduces variance


lambda, alpha (XGBoost L2/L1)
Direct regularisation on leaf weights


n_estimators (RF/XGBoost)
More trees reduce variance (RF) or require early stopping (XGBoost)





5. Feature Importance Stability (SHAP Variance Across Folds)
A well-generalised model should assign consistent importance to the same features across different CV folds. If SHAP value rankings change substantially from fold to fold, the model is overfitting to idiosyncratic patterns in each training partition.
Practical check: compute SHAP values for each CV fold; report the mean and standard deviation of each feature’s mean |SHAP|. Features with high standard deviation relative to their mean importance are contributing noise, not signal.


6. Remote-Sensing-Specific Overfitting Risks
Saturation in high-biomass forests: Field plots with AGB > 300 Mg ha⁻¹ are rare in most datasets. A model that memorises these extreme observations performs well on training data but generalises poorly to unseen high-biomass stands. Detecting this: plot residuals vs. observed AGB — if large residuals cluster at high AGB only in the test set, saturation-driven overfitting is likely.
Spectral collinearity: Optical datasets (Landsat 8 bands, Sentinel-2 12 bands) are highly correlated. High VIF (Variance Inflation Factor > 10) among predictors inflates coefficient variance in linear models and destabilises feature importance in tree models. Remedies: PCA preprocessing, Lasso, or explicit VIF filtering.
Spatial pseudoreplication (see also Spatial CV above): Spatially proximate training and test points share similar spectral and structural properties, creating the illusion of high accuracy. Random k-fold CV inflates \(R^2\) by 0.1–0.3 in LiDAR AGB models with high spatial autocorrelation. Spatial block CV or BLOO-CV is mandatory.






Tip



A complete overfitting checklist for AGB / LST / NPP models:

Report \(\Delta R^2\) and \(\Delta\text{RMSE}\) (train vs. spatial-CV test)
Use spatial block CV or BLOO-CV — never random k-fold alone
Check learning curves: does validation RMSE plateau far above training RMSE?
Apply regularisation (Lasso / Ridge / ElasticNet) or tune tree complexity
Check SHAP stability across CV folds for top-ranked features
Plot residuals vs. predicted and vs. key covariates (especially AGB range)
Check VIF among predictors; remove or decorrelate features with VIF > 10







AIC / BIC — Model Selection Criteria
\[\text{AIC} = 2k - 2\ln(\hat{L}), \qquad \text{BIC} = k\ln(n) - 2\ln(\hat{L})\]
where \(k\) = number of parameters, \(n\) = sample size, \(\hat{L}\) = maximized likelihood.
Interpretation: Both penalize model complexity to prevent overfitting. Lower AIC/BIC = better model. BIC penalizes complexity more strongly than AIC for \(n > 7\).
\(\Delta\)AIC rules of thumb: - \(\Delta\)AIC < 2 — models are statistically equivalent - \(\Delta\)AIC 4–7 — some evidence for the lower-AIC model - \(\Delta\)AIC > 10 — strong evidence the lower-AIC model is better
Common use: Comparing mixed-effects model structures for biomass–canopy relationships; selecting predictor sets in NPP–climate regression; choosing between spatial autocorrelation model structures.

title: Process-Based Models
text:
Process-based models (PBMs) represent ecosystem and environmental behavior through explicit mathematical formulations of physical, chemical, and biological processes. Rather than fitting empirical relationships to observed data, PBMs encode mechanistic understanding of how and why systems function — using differential equations and energy/mass balance constraints derived from first principles. This makes them uniquely suited to extrapolation beyond observed conditions, scenario analysis, and the study of cross-scale feedbacks that purely statistical methods cannot recover.




Mechanistic interpretability — parameters correspond to measurable physical and biological quantities (Vcmax, aerodynamic roughness length, decomposition rates), making outputs traceable and falsifiable
Extrapolation to novel conditions — mechanistic constraints prevent unrealistic predictions outside the observational range; critical for climate-change projections
Captures feedbacks — vegetation–climate–soil and urban canopy–atmosphere feedbacks are embedded in the model structure, not inferred post hoc
Enables scenario analysis — a consistent framework for comparing SSP126 vs. SSP585, management interventions, green infrastructure designs, or disturbance regimes
Process attribution — individual process contributions (e.g., transpiration vs. albedo cooling; GPP vs. respiration) can be isolated by turning model components on or off






Parameter uncertainty — many parameters (Vcmax, turnover times, aerodynamic roughness, allocation fractions) are poorly constrained globally and require calibration
Structural uncertainty — different formulations of the same process (e.g., stomatal conductance schemes) produce divergent predictions even with identical inputs
Computational cost — global DGVMs at fine spatial resolution and 3D urban CFD models both require substantial computing resources
Missing processes — nutrient cycling, mycorrhizal networks, hydraulic failure under drought, and fine-scale urban morphology are still poorly represented in many models
Rigid assumptions — fixed plant functional types and parameterizations may not capture local adaptation or rapid vegetation change

title: Process-Based Models
text:
2 · Vegetation Process-Based Models
Vegetation PBMs simulate the coupled cycles of carbon, water, energy, and nutrients across scales ranging from individual tree plots to the global land surface. At their core, photosynthesis (GPP) follows the Farquhar–von Caemmerer–Berry (FvCB) biochemical scheme; GPP minus autotrophic respiration yields NPP; NPP minus heterotrophic decomposition yields NEE. Water balance links Penman–Monteith evapotranspiration to soil moisture and runoff. At larger scales, vegetation composition and structure are themselves dynamic state variables that respond to and feed back on climate.


Dynamic Global Vegetation Models (DGVMs)
Dynamic Global Vegetation Models (DGVMs) are among the tools I am most interested in for projecting terrestrial ecosystem responses to climate change across regional to global scales, as they simulate vegetation dynamics, competition, mortality, and disturbance processes. Core processes simulated:







Process
Key formulation




Leaf-level photosynthesis
FvCB scheme (Vcmax, Jmax, mesophyll conductance)


Stomatal conductance
Ball–Berry or Medlyn optimization framework


Carbon allocation
Fixed or dynamic partitioning to leaf, wood, root, and seed pools


Phenology
Temperature / day-length / chilling-day thresholds


Mortality
Carbon starvation, hydraulic failure, background turnover


Disturbance
Fire (SPITFIRE), gap dynamics, land-use change



Major models in this family include LPJ-GUESS, CLM-FATES, ED2, ORCHIDEE, and JULES. These models are widely used in terrestrial ecosystem and carbon cycle research, including multi-model intercomparison projects such as TRENDY, which contributes to the Global Carbon Budget. Several are also coupled with CMIP6 Earth System Models (ESMs) to simulate land–atmosphere interactions under SSP climate scenarios (e.g., SSP1-2.6 to SSP5-8.5). DGVMs are particularly well suited for long-term climate impact assessment, regional carbon budget attribution, and studies of land–atmosphere feedbacks.
DGVMs represent vegetation as a mixture of Plant Functional Types (PFTs) — such as broadleaf deciduous trees, C4 grasses, and boreal conifers — each defined by distinct photosynthetic, phenological, and hydraulic traits. Within each grid cell, PFTs compete for light, water, and nutrients, while their fractional cover changes over time through processes including growth, mortality, and disturbance.



Forest Gap Models
Gap models — including SORTIE and FORMIND — simulate individual tree birth, growth, competition for light, and mortality within small plots (~0.01–1 ha). They resolve size-structured competition and successional dynamics over decades to centuries following disturbance (fire, logging, insect outbreak). Best suited for stand-scale biodiversity–productivity analysis and forest succession studies.



3-PG — Physiological Principles Predicting Growth
3-PG is a parsimonious process-based model driven by monthly climate inputs (temperature, precipitation, radiation, VPD) and soil water-holding capacity. It simulates forest stand growth and biomass production using a light-use efficiency (fAPAR × ε) framework modified by temperature, VPD, and water-stress modifiers. Widely used in plantation forestry and timber yield estimation due to its low data requirements and strong empirical validation base.

title: Process-Based Models
section: 3 · Cooling Effect of Urban Green Space — Process-Based Models
text:
3 · Cooling Effect of Urban Green Space — Process-Based Models
Urban green spaces cool cities through three coupled physical pathways: (1) evapotranspiration — latent heat flux removes energy as water vapor; (2) shading — tree canopies intercept solar and longwave radiation, reducing surface and air temperatures; and (3) airflow and convective heat exchange — vegetation modifies wind speed, turbulence, and the aerodynamic coupling between surfaces and the overlying atmosphere, governing how efficiently sensible heat is transported away. These three pathways interact: dense canopies that maximize shading can simultaneously reduce wind speed and suppress convective cooling, while open park configurations may enhance advective cooling from cooler air into surrounding streets.
Urban morphology — the geometry and arrangement of buildings — is an equally critical but often underappreciated control on the thermal environment. Building height, street canyon aspect ratio (H/W), and block layout determine how solar radiation penetrates to street level, how longwave heat is trapped within canyons, and how strongly ambient wind is channeled, decelerated, or deflected before reaching green spaces. A narrow, deep street canyon with tall buildings on both sides traps heat through repeated longwave re-emission between walls (the urban canyon effect) and simultaneously shelters the canyon floor from wind, suppressing convective heat removal. Conversely, wide boulevards or irregular open-block layouts promote wind penetration and allow cool park air to advect into adjacent built areas. The sky-view factor (SVF) — the fraction of the sky hemisphere visible from a surface — integrates these geometric effects: low SVF indicates a deeply enclosed canyon with reduced longwave cooling at night, while high SVF allows more effective radiative heat loss. Building materials further modulate storage heat flux (ΔQS): high thermal mass concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, extending thermal stress well beyond sunset. Process-based models therefore need to represent not only vegetation properties but also the surrounding built fabric — its height distribution, plan density, wall/roof albedo, and thermal mass — to accurately attribute how much cooling green space can realistically deliver within a given urban context.
Process-based models vary in how explicitly they resolve each pathway. CFD-based models (ENVI-met) fully couple vegetation, airflow, and building geometry at the microscale; energy-balance models (SUEWS, TRM) parameterize convection through aerodynamic resistance derived from urban morphology metrics; mesoscale models (WRF-Urban, CLMU) represent canyon geometry and building drag to resolve city-to-atmosphere feedbacks. Inventory-based tools (i-Tree Eco) estimate cooling from leaf area and microclimate records without explicit building geometry.


ENVI-met
A 3D microscale model (0.5–5 m resolution) that solves fully coupled atmospheric dynamics, radiation transfer, and soil–vegetation equations. It explicitly resolves turbulent airflow around building facades and within tree canopies using a k-ε turbulence closure, computes convective heat exchange at every surface via forced- and natural-convection coefficients, and models leaf boundary-layer resistance as a function of local wind speed. This makes ENVI-met uniquely capable of capturing the interplay between canopy shading, wind channeling through street canyons, and pedestrian-level thermal comfort. Computationally expensive; primarily used for small-domain (<1 km²) green infrastructure design.



SUEWS — Surface Urban Energy and Water Balance Scheme
A neighborhood- to city-scale surface energy balance model (100 m – 1 km) partitioning net radiation into sensible heat (QH), latent heat (QE), storage heat (ΔQS), and anthropogenic heat (QF). Convective exchange is parameterized through bulk aerodynamic transfer coefficients derived from urban roughness length and displacement height; the aerodynamic resistance (ra) linking surface to reference-level air adjusts for atmospheric stability (Monin–Obukhov similarity). ET is calculated via Penman–Monteith for each urban surface type (vegetation, pavement, water). Open-source and validated at flux tower sites globally; capable of multi-decadal runs.



WRF-Urban
A mesoscale model (1–10 km) coupling the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) atmosphere with urban canopy schemes (SLUCM, BEP, BEM). WRF-Urban resolves mesoscale wind circulations — urban–rural breezes, heat island–driven convergence zones, and nocturnal drainage flows — that govern city-scale advective heat transport. The Building Effect Parameterization (BEP) explicitly represents drag, turbulent kinetic energy, and convective fluxes within the urban canopy layer. Best suited for evaluating city-wide cooling strategies and projecting UHI intensity under future climate scenarios.



CLMU — Community Land Model Urban (CLM5 / CESM)
The urban module embedded in CLM5, representing cities as a canyon geometry (roof, sunlit/shaded walls, impervious road, pervious ground). It solves the full energy, water, and radiation balance for each surface type, with multi-layer thermal mass for building walls and roofs. Turbulent exchange between canyon surfaces and the overlying atmosphere is handled via CLM5’s surface-layer scheme (Zeng–Dickinson stability functions), coupling convective heat fluxes to the CESM atmosphere. Enables global/regional UHI simulation under CMIP6 SSP scenarios. Described in Oleson et al. (2010) and Lawrence et al. (2019).



TRM — Two-Resistance Mechanistic Model
A physically based analytical model that partitions urban vegetation cooling into latent and sensible heat fluxes via two resistances: aerodynamic resistance (ra, which encodes convective efficiency — governed by wind speed, roughness length, and atmospheric stability) and surface/stomatal resistance (rs, governed by LAI, VPD, and soil moisture):
\[\lambda E = \frac{\rho c_p}{\gamma} \cdot \frac{e_s(T_s) - e_a}{r_a + r_s}, \qquad H = \rho c_p \cdot \frac{T_s - T_a}{r_a}\]
The ra term explicitly links wind-driven convection to cooling: in low-wind, stable conditions ra rises and sensible heat dissipation is suppressed; in ventilated parks or street canyons with strong airflow, ra falls and convective cooling is enhanced. When rs is low (well-watered, open stomata), energy partitions to latent heat cooling; under drought stress rs rises and the burden shifts to convective sensible heat. Compatible with thermal remote sensing (Landsat, ECOSTRESS) for spatially continuous Ts inputs. Lightweight — runs at full satellite resolution city-wide without CFD or mesoscale compute cost.



i-Tree Eco
A USDA Forest Service tool that quantifies urban tree ecosystem services — cooling, carbon storage, air pollution removal, and stormwater interception — from field inventory data (species, DBH, crown dimensions) combined with local climate and hourly wind speed records. ET-based cooling is scaled to individual tree leaf area via a modified Penman–Monteith equation; sensible heat removal through convective exchange is estimated from crown surface area and local air temperature gradients. Outputs are expressed in physical units and monetary value (USD), making it the standard tool for city governments and urban forest managers.

library(neonUtilities)

  project("EPSG:4326")           # reproject to WGS84

section: Step 5 — Download 3DEP LiDAR and Build CHM
text:
Step 5 — Download 3DEP LiDAR and Build CHM
3DEP point cloud tiles for Virginia are available from USGS TNM. The Shenandoah Valley area (including SCBI) was acquired under the VA Statewide 2017 project at ~2–8 pts/m².

library(httr); library(jsonlite); library(lidR)

# Query 3DEP tiles
tnm_url <- paste0(
  "https://tnmaccess.nationalmap.gov/api/v1/products?",
  "datasets=Lidar+Point+Cloud+%283DEP%29&",
  "bbox=", scbi$lon_min, ",", scbi$lat_min, ",",
           scbi$lon_max, ",", scbi$lat_max,
  "&outputFormat=JSON&max=20"
)
tiles <- fromJSON(content(GET(tnm_url), "text"))
cat("3DEP tiles available:", tiles$total,
    "| Acquisition:", unique(tiles$items$moreInfo), "\n")

dir.create("data/3dep_scbi", showWarnings=FALSE)
for (url in tiles$items$downloadURL) {
  f <- file.path("data/3dep_scbi", basename(url))
  if (!file.exists(f)) download.file(url, f, mode="wb", quiet=TRUE)
}

# Build CHM using lidR
ctg <- readLAScatalog("data/3dep_scbi/")
opt_chunk_buffer(ctg) <- 15
ctg_norm <- normalize_height(ctg, knnidw(k=8, p=2))
chm_3dep  <- rasterize_canopy(ctg_norm, res=1,
               algorithm=pitfree(c(0,2,5,10,15,20), c(0,1.5))) |>
  project("EPSG:4326")

section: Step 6 — Extract CHM at GEDI Footprint Locations
text:
Step 6 — Extract CHM at GEDI Footprint Locations
Each GEDI footprint is ~25 m in diameter. We buffer each footprint centroid by 12.5 m and extract the mean CHM within that buffer — matching the GEDI spatial averaging.

library(exactextractr)

gedi_sf  <- st_as_sf(scbi_clean, coords=c("lon","lat"), crs=4326) |>
  st_transform(32617)   # UTM Zone 17N for metric buffering
gedi_buf <- st_buffer(gedi_sf, dist=12.5)

scbi_clean$neon_chm <- exact_extract(
  chm_neon |> project("EPSG:32617"), gedi_buf, fun="mean")

scbi_clean$dep_chm  <- exact_extract(
  chm_3dep |> project("EPSG:32617"), gedi_buf, fun="mean")

# Keep only footprints with valid CHM in both sources
scbi_comp <- scbi_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(neon_chm), !is.na(dep_chm),
         neon_chm > 2, dep_chm > 2)

text:
Results

Spatial Distribution — Footprints by Zone


Each dot is a quality-passing GEDI footprint. The green dashed box marks the Central Park boundary. Lower Manhattan and Midtown show the most mixed signal — tall buildings, low streets, and occasional small parks all within the same 0.12° × 0.09° window.




Interactive Map — Surface Classification









RH95 by Urban Zone


Central Park shows the tallest and most consistent RH95 (~20 m), entirely from tree canopy. Lower Manhattan has the highest mean RH95 (~60 m) — but this reflects skyscraper rooftops, not trees. North Manhattan and the Upper West/East Side cluster around 15–20 m, a mix of street trees and low apartment buildings.




Waveform Width (RH95 − RH25) — The Key Diagnostic
The waveform width (RH95 − RH25) captures how spread out the returned energy is vertically:

Trees: wide spread — laser penetrates through the canopy and still gets returns from the ground and understory (low RH25), while the top return comes from the canopy surface (high RH95)
Buildings: narrow spread — a flat rooftop concentrates almost all returns at one height; RH25 is nearly as high as RH95
Streets: near-zero — all returns from the ground



This single metric can act as a building/vegetation separator without any external data: footprints with waveform_width > 10 m are almost exclusively vegetation; those with waveform_width < 5 m are likely buildings or streets. A threshold of ~8 m gives a practical first-pass filter.




Full RH Profile Comparison


The RH25–RH95 profile shape differs fundamentally between surface types. For vegetation, RH25 stays low (ground/understory) while RH75 and RH95 jump sharply — a signature of a closed-canopy forest. For buildings, all four percentiles step upward uniformly, tracking the roof height. For streets, all percentiles hover near zero.




GEDI RH95 vs OSM Building Height


GEDI RH95 tracks building height but systematically underestimates — increasingly so for tall buildings. A 10 m brownstone might yield RH95 ≈ 9 m (small underestimate), but a 200 m skyscraper might yield RH95 ≈ 170 m. The underestimate arises because the ~25 m GEDI footprint inevitably overlaps a street edge at building corners, diluting the roof-level return with near-ground signal.




Quality Flag Pass Rate


Vegetation footprints pass QC at ~88 % — the GEDI waveform decomposition algorithm was designed for forest returns. Building and street footprints pass at ~44–50 %: the algorithm flags the abnormal waveform shapes (sharp single-return peaks from rooftops; very weak returns from roads) as unreliable. After quality filtering, urban datasets are dominated by vegetation and mixed-footprint shots, which partially self-corrects the building contamination problem.

Key Takeaways

Waveform width is a free diagnostic: RH95 − RH25 > 8–10 m strongly indicates vegetation; < 5 m indicates a flat built surface.
Quality filtering is biased toward vegetation: Buildings naturally fail QC at higher rates, so standard GEDI pipelines inadvertently self-filter some building contamination.
Underestimation scales with building height: GEDI systematically underestimates tall buildings because the footprint always samples some street-level signal at roof edges.
Urban GEDI is most reliable inside parks: Central Park footprints are clean and vegetation-dominated after standard quality filtering.
Combine GEDI with OSM or land-cover masks for fully rigorous urban analyses — especially when building heights > 20 m are common.

title: Pre-Processing Airborne LiDAR Data: lidR vs lasR vs Python
text: Airborne LiDAR point clouds are rarely analysis-ready out of the box. Raw tiles from 3DEP, NEON AOP, or proprietary acquisitions often carry noise, inconsistent densities across acquisition campaigns, and missing height normalization. This post documents a reproducible pipeline covering every stage from raw LAS/LAZ ingestion to a clean, normalized, decimated cloud — shown side by side in lidR, lasR, and Python.

title: Pre-Processing Airborne LiDAR Data: lidR vs lasR vs Python
section: Part 1: Pre-Processing Pipeline — Stage by Stage
text:
Part 1: Pre-Processing Pipeline — Stage by Stage

Stage 1 — Input & Setup

lidRlasRPython


library(lidR)

ctg <- readLAScatalog("path/to/las_folder/")

opt_filter(ctg)       <- "-drop_class 7 18"   # drop noise classes on read
opt_chunk_buffer(ctg) <- 10                    # 10 m buffer for SOR edge safety
opt_chunk_size(ctg)   <- 500                   # 500 × 500 m chunks

plot(ctg, mapview = TRUE)   # visual tile overview
summary(ctg)                # density, CRS, point count per tile


library(lasR)

# No catalog object in lasR.
# The folder path goes directly to exec().
# Filter, buffer, and chunk size are exec() arguments.

read_stage <- reader_las(filter = "-drop_class 7 18")


import laspy
import numpy as np
from pathlib import Path
import glob, json
import pdal

# ── laspy approach: list tiles manually ────────────────────────────
laz_files = sorted(glob.glob("path/to/las_folder/*.laz"))

# Quick density check on first tile
with laspy.open(laz_files[0]) as f:
    las   = f.read()
    area  = (las.x.max() - las.x.min()) * (las.y.max() - las.y.min())
    dens  = len(las.x) / area
    print(f"Tile density: {dens:.1f} pts/m²")

# ── PDAL approach: process folder via exec loop ────────────────────
# (PDAL has no catalog object; tiles are iterated in Python)









NoteStage 1 — Pros & Cons















lidR
lasR
Python




Pros
LAScatalog gives per-tile density map and CRS check; plot() reveals coverage gaps instantly
No catalog boilerplate; folder path to exec() is all that is needed
Pure Python — no R dependency; laspy is lightweight; integrates with pathlib/glob for custom filtering


Cons
Catalog scan reads all file headers — slow for thousands of tiles; buffer must be explicitly remembered
No visual tile overview; hard to spot corrupt or outlier-density tiles before the run
No built-in catalog with visual tile map; tile iteration and buffering must be coded manually; laspy loads the entire tile into memory









Stage 2 — Ground Classification (if missing)

lidRlasRPython


has_ground <- function(las) any(las@data$Classification == LASGROUND)

classify_ground_csf <- function(las) {
  if (!has_ground(las))
    las <- classify_ground(las, csf(sloop_smooth     = TRUE,
                                    class_threshold  = 0.5,
                                    cloth_resolution = 0.5,
                                    time_step        = 0.65))
  return(las)
}

opt_output_files(ctg) <- paste0(tempdir(), "/{*}_ground")
ctg_ground <- catalog_apply(ctg, classify_ground_csf)


# lasR has no per-tile conditional — CSF runs on all tiles unconditionally.
# Safe for 3DEP (re-classifying pre-labelled ground is harmless).

ground_stage <- classify_ground(
  csf(sloop_smooth     = TRUE,
      class_threshold  = 0.5,
      cloth_resolution = 0.5,
      time_step        = 0.65)
)


# ── Option A: CSF Python package ──────────────────────────────────
# pip install cloth-simulation-filter
import CSF

def classify_ground_csf(las):
    """Return a boolean mask of ground points using CSF."""
    pts = np.column_stack([las.x, las.y, las.z])

    c = CSF.CSF()
    c.params.bSloopSmooth    = True
    c.params.cloth_resolution = 0.5
    c.params.class_threshold  = 0.5
    c.params.time_step        = 0.65

    c.setPointCloud(pts.tolist())
    ground_idx     = CSF.VecInt()
    non_ground_idx = CSF.VecInt()
    c.do_filtering(ground_idx, non_ground_idx)

    mask = np.zeros(len(las.x), dtype=bool)
    mask[list(ground_idx)] = True
    return mask   # True = ground

# Apply only if no Class 2 exists
if not np.any(las.classification == 2):
    ground_mask = classify_ground_csf(las)
    las.classification[ground_mask] = 2

# ── Option B: PDAL filters.csf (used in full pipeline below) ──────
csf_stage = {
    "type":       "filters.csf",
    "smooth":     True,
    "resolution": 0.5,
    "threshold":  0.5
}









NoteStage 2 — Pros & Cons















lidR
lasR
Python




Pros
Conditional has_ground skips CSF on pre-classified 3DEP tiles — saves time; can visualize ground on one tile interactively before batch-running
C++ CSF is the fastest of the three; seamlessly chained into the pipeline
CSF Python package mirrors the original C++ algorithm exactly; PDAL’s filters.csf is equally fast; both integrate naturally into numpy workflows


Cons
catalog_apply() with a custom function is verbose; R-level loop overhead
No conditional — CSF always runs even on pre-classified tiles
CSF package requires tolist() conversion (Python list, not numpy array); less maintained than lidR/lasR CSF implementations; PDAL JSON config is verbose









Stage 3 — Height Normalization

lidRlasRPython


normalize_and_save <- function(las) {
  dtm <- rasterize_terrain(las, res = 1, algorithm = knnidw(k = 10, p = 2))
  las <- normalize_height(las, dtm)

  # Save height as named extra-bytes attribute BEFORE restoring raw Z
  las <- add_lasattribute(las, las@data$Z, "Height", "Height above ground (m)")
  las <- unnormalize_height(las)   # Z → raw elevation; Height persists

  las <- filter_poi(las, Height > -0.5 & Height < 80)
  return(las)
}

opt_output_files(ctg) <- paste0(tempdir(), "/{*}_norm")
ctg_norm <- catalog_apply(ctg_ground, normalize_and_save)


# normalize() builds DTM and subtracts it in one streaming pass.
# Z is overwritten (normalized in place).

norm_stage <- normalize(knnidw(k = 10, p = 2))

# Height filter on the now-normalized Z
filt_stage <- filter_poi(keep_z_above(-0.5) & keep_z_below(80))

# To preserve raw Z alongside Height: run a first-pass stage to copy Z
# into an extra-bytes attribute before normalization, then normalize.
save_raw_z <- add_extrabytes("float", "RawZ", "Raw elevation (m a.s.l.)")


from scipy.spatial import cKDTree

def normalize_height(las, k=10, p=2):
    """Build kNN-IDW DTM from ground points and compute height above ground."""
    gnd = las.classification == 2
    gx, gy, gz = las.x[gnd], las.y[gnd], las.z[gnd]

    # k-NN inverse-distance weighted interpolation
    tree   = cKDTree(np.column_stack([gx, gy]))
    dists, idx = tree.query(np.column_stack([las.x, las.y]), k=k)
    dists  = np.where(dists == 0, 1e-10, dists)   # avoid division by zero
    w      = dists ** (-p)
    ground_elev = (w * gz[idx]).sum(axis=1) / w.sum(axis=1)

    height = las.z - ground_elev

    # Save as extra-bytes attribute (preserves raw Z unchanged)
    las.add_extra_dim(laspy.ExtraBytesParams(
        name="Height", type=np.float32,
        description="Height above ground (m)"))
    las.Height = height.astype(np.float32)

    # Filter artifacts
    keep = (las.Height > -0.5) & (las.Height < 80)
    return las[keep]

# ── PDAL equivalent (used in full pipeline) ───────────────────────
hag_stage = {
    "type":  "filters.hag_nn",   # Height Above Ground via nearest neighbours
    "count": 10
}
# PDAL stores result in HeightAboveGround dimension; raw Z is preserved.
filt_stage_pdal = {
    "type":   "filters.range",
    "limits": "HeightAboveGround[-0.5:80]"
}









NoteStage 3 — Pros & Cons















lidR
lasR
Python




Pros
add_lasattribute() + unnormalize_height() keeps both raw Z and Height in one pass — no second run needed; DTM inspectable as a raster
One-pass streaming — DTM is never materialised in full memory; fastest of the three
PDAL’s filters.hag_nn is simple and preserves raw Z automatically; laspy + scipy gives full control over interpolation method and edge handling


Cons
Full DTM raster materialised in R memory before normalization; slow for large dense tiles
Z is overwritten — recovering raw elevation needs a pre-pass to copy Z into extra bytes
scipy kNN IDW is ~3× slower than lidR’s C++ implementation for dense tiles; tile-edge artefacts require manual buffering in the laspy approach









Stage 4 — Statistical Outlier Removal (SOR)

lidRlasRPython


remove_noise_sor <- function(las) {
  las <- classify_noise(las, sor(k = 15, m = 3))    # labels, does not remove
  las <- filter_poi(las, Classification != LASNOISE) # then remove
  return(las)
}

# Buffer already set on ctg (opt_chunk_buffer = 10)
opt_output_files(ctg) <- paste0(tempdir(), "/{*}_clean")
ctg_clean <- catalog_apply(ctg_norm, remove_noise_sor)


sor_stage <- classify_noise(sor(k = 15, m = 3))
# buffer = 10 is passed to exec() — applies automatically to this stage


def sor_filter(las, k=15, m=3, use_height=True):
    """Statistical Outlier Removal on 3D point coordinates."""
    z_col = las.Height if (use_height and hasattr(las, "Height")) else las.z
    pts   = np.column_stack([las.x, las.y, z_col])

    tree  = cKDTree(pts)
    # Query k+1 (first result is the point itself, dist=0)
    dists, _ = tree.query(pts, k=k + 1)
    mean_dists = dists[:, 1:].mean(axis=1)   # exclude self

    mu, sigma = mean_dists.mean(), mean_dists.std()
    keep = mean_dists <= mu + m * sigma
    return las[keep]

las = sor_filter(las, k=15, m=3)

# ── PDAL equivalent ────────────────────────────────────────────────
sor_stage_pdal = {
    "type":       "filters.outlier",

def voxel_decimate(las, res=0.447):

             "filename":   outfile,
             "extra_dims": "HeightAboveGround=float32"}

# Batch process all tiles
for infile in sorted(glob.glob("path/to/las_folder/*.laz")):
    outfile = infile.replace("las_folder", "output")
    p = pdal.Pipeline(json.dumps(make_pipeline(infile, outfile)))

1.1 Random Thinning

{"type": "filters.sample", "radius": 0.316}   # approx. 10 pts/m²

current_dens = len(las.x) / ((las.x.max()-las.x.min())*(las.y.max()-las.y.min()))

Each point is independently retained with probability \(p = d_{\text{target}}/d_{\text{local}}\). Spatially blind — dense clusters stay dense.
Strengths: fastest; no discretisation artifacts; preserves attribute distributions. Weaknesses: no spatial uniformity; density gradients persist; result depends on random seed.



1.2 Voxel Thinning

    key = (np.floor(las.x/res).astype(np.int64) * 1_000_000_007 +
           np.floor(las.y/res).astype(np.int64) * 7_001 +
           np.floor(las.z/res).astype(np.int64))
    _, idx = np.unique(key, return_index=True)
    return las[np.sort(idx)]



Divides 3D space into cubic voxels; retains one random point per occupied voxel.
Strengths: 3D spatial uniformity; removes density gradients from scan-angle overlap; best for mixed 3DEP campaigns. Weaknesses: fine-scale vertical structure within a voxel may be lost; no direct pts/m² targeting.



1.3 Homogenize Thinning

lidRlasRPython


las <- decimate_points(las, homogenize(density = 10, res = 5))


decim <- sampling_homogenize(density = 10, res = 5)


# No direct PDAL equivalent — implement with numpy 2D grid
def homogenize_decimate(las, target_density=10, cell_res=5):
    xi = np.floor(las.x / cell_res).astype(int)
    yi = np.floor(las.y / cell_res).astype(int)
    keep = np.zeros(len(las.x), dtype=bool)
    cell_area = cell_res ** 2
    max_pts   = int(target_density * cell_area)
    for (cx, cy), idx in _group_by(xi, yi):
        chosen = np.random.choice(idx, min(len(idx), max_pts), replace=False)
        keep[chosen] = True
    return las[keep]

def _group_by(xi, yi):
    from itertools import groupby
    pairs = sorted(zip(zip(xi, yi), np.arange(len(xi))), key=lambda x: x[0])
    for key, group in groupby(pairs, key=lambda x: x[0]):
        yield key, [g[1] for g in group]



2D cells randomly thinned to density pts/m²; cells below target are left untouched.
Strengths: explicit pts/m² target; removes horizontal density gradients; preserves full vertical structure. Weaknesses: 3D vertical clustering can persist; Python implementation requires more code.

# numpy approach — preserves all LAS attributes
def highest_point(las, res=1.0):
    xi  = np.floor(las.x / res).astype(int)
    yi  = np.floor(las.y / res).astype(int)
    key = xi * 1_000_000_007 + yi
    # For each unique (xi, yi) cell, keep the index of the highest Z
    order = np.lexsort((las.z, key))          # sort by key then z
    _, last_in_group = np.unique(key[order], return_index=True)  # last = highest z
    return las[order[last_in_group]]

def lowest_point(las, res=1.0):
    xi  = np.floor(las.x / res).astype(int)
    yi  = np.floor(las.y / res).astype(int)
    key = xi * 1_000_000_007 + yi
    order = np.lexsort((-las.z, key))         # sort by key then -z (ascending z last)
    _, first_in_group = np.unique(key[order], return_index=True)
    return las[order[first_in_group]]

Aims:
Integrate field investigations, remote sensing, and modeling to reveal cross-scale mechanisms, thereby supporting the development of robust models for understanding ecosystems — particularly forests — and improving forest management to enhance human well-being.


Forest above ground biomass estimation
How to estimate forest AGB across large spatial scale?

LiDAR-based modeling of forest above-ground biomass (AGB) using USGS 3DEP and NEON airborne point clouds, integrated with GEDI spaceborne LiDAR footprints and ESA CCI Biomass products for cross-scale validation. Built a large-scale processing pipeline that derives canopy structure metrics (height percentiles, density, rumple index) and predicts plot-level AGB with Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and stacked ensemble models, evaluated with grouped cross-validation and SHAP-based interpretation.
Tools: R (lidR, lasR, terra, sf), Python (scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, SHAP)
